questions.q: The 1881 assassination of President James Garfield by a disappointed office seeker strengthened public support for which reform?
options: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890
The Interstate Commerce Act, passed by Congress in 1887
The Dawes Severalty Act of 1887
The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883
questions.explain: Charles Guiteau's crime made the spoils system look dangerous. Congress responded with the Pendleton Act, which tied some federal jobs to merit exams.

questions.q: The Pendleton Act of 1883 began to fill some federal jobs through which method?
options: Seniority ranking among Civil War veterans only
Recommendations from members of Congress
Patronage appointments made by the party in power
Competitive civil service examinations
questions.explain: The law aimed to replace patronage with merit, so qualified applicants could win some government posts by passing tests.

questions.q: Which agency did the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 create to oversee railroad rates?
options: The Federal Trade Commission
The Railroad Labor Board
The Bureau of Corporations
The Interstate Commerce Commission
questions.explain: Farmers and shippers had complained of unfair rates and rebates. The act made railroads charge reasonable rates and set up the ICC, an early federal regulatory body.

questions.q: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 declared illegal which kind of business practice?
options: Interlocking directorates between competing firms
Secret rebates and rate discrimination by railroads
Tariffs on imported raw materials
Combinations and contracts in restraint of trade
questions.explain: The law targeted trusts that choked off competition. Vague wording and narrow court rulings limited its early effectiveness.

questions.q: Which New York political machine was led by William "Boss" Tweed in the 1860s and early 1870s?
options: The Albany Regency
Tammany Hall
The Mugwumps
The Bucktails
questions.explain: Tweed's ring used patronage and inflated contracts to steal huge sums. Cartoons by Thomas Nast helped turn the public against it.

questions.q: The cartoonist Thomas Nast is best remembered in Gilded Age politics for attacking whom?
options: The Tweed Ring of New York City
The Carnegie Steel Company
The Farmers' Alliance
The Knights of Labor
questions.explain: Nast's drawings in Harper's Weekly mocked Tweed and his associates and helped bring about the ring's downfall and Tweed's conviction.

questions.q: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 was significant because it was the first major federal law to...
options: Ban all immigration from Asia
Require every immigrant to pass a literacy test
Set a numerical quota for each nation of origin
Bar immigrants of one nationality from entering the country
questions.explain: Congress banned Chinese laborers for ten years, setting a precedent for restricting immigration by nationality or race.

questions.q: Which developments in the American West helped fuel anti-Chinese agitation that led to the Exclusion Act?
options: Job competition and racial prejudice in hard times
Growing Chinese ownership of Western banks and mines
Chinese workers' open support for the Populist Party
Complaints from railroad owners about Chinese laborers
questions.explain: Chinese laborers had built railroads and mined gold, but in the hard times of the 1870s many white workers blamed them for low wages and pushed for exclusion.

questions.q: In Chae Chan Ping v. United States (1889), the Supreme Court upheld Chinese exclusion by reasoning that...
options: Earlier treaties with China had no legal force at all
The Fourteenth Amendment barred Asian residents from ever entering the country
The national government holds broad power over immigration
Each state alone could decide who was allowed to enter
questions.explain: The Court treated control over immigration as part of national sovereignty, giving Congress wide authority even when it contradicted earlier treaties.

questions.q: The Chinese Exclusion Acts were repealed in 1943. What wartime circumstance helped bring this about?
options: A peace treaty between China and Japan required repeal
China was a US ally against Japan
A Chinese boycott of American goods forced Congress to act
The Supreme Court had ruled the exclusion laws unconstitutional
questions.explain: With China fighting Japan alongside the United States, continuing exclusion embarrassed the government. Repeal allowed a very small annual quota.

questions.q: The Dawes Act of 1887 aimed to change Native American life by...
options: Relocating eastern tribes west of the Mississippi River
Dividing tribal land into individual allotments
Restoring tribal self-government under elected councils
Ending federal recognition of tribes as legal entities
questions.explain: Reformers hoped private farms would assimilate Native people. In practice allotment cut tribal land holdings drastically as surplus acreage was sold.

questions.q: What was a major long-term result of the Dawes Act for Native nations?
options: Growth of tribal land holdings
A sharp loss of land held by tribes
Full citizenship for every tribal member in 1887
Return of the Black Hills to the Lakota
questions.explain: Allotments broke up communally held land, and the leftover land was opened to non-Native buyers, shrinking the Native land base.

questions.q: Carlisle Indian Industrial School, founded in 1879, reflected which federal approach to Native children?
options: Support for preserving tribal languages
Education delivered only on reservations by elders
Removal of tribes to Indian Territory
Forced assimilation through boarding schools
questions.explain: Founder Richard Henry Pratt wanted to erase Native cultures. Students were given new names and clothing and were punished for speaking their languages.

questions.q: The 1890 massacre at Wounded Knee Creek took place in which present-day state?
options: Montana
Oklahoma
Wyoming
South Dakota
questions.explain: The 7th Cavalry killed at least 150 Lakota, many of them women and children, near the Pine Ridge Reservation. It is often seen as the end of the Plains wars.

questions.q: The Ghost Dance movement among Plains peoples in 1890 was a response to...
options: Anger at the arrival of new missionary schools
Excitement over a railroad boom in western Kansas
Hope that Oklahoma would soon open to settlers
Despair over reservation life and loss of land
questions.explain: The Ghost Dance promised renewal of Native life. Alarmed officials feared it would spark an uprising, which set the stage for the tragedy at Wounded Knee.

questions.q: The gold rush in the Black Hills in the 1870s led to war with which people, whose treaty land it was?
options: The Navajo
The Seminole
The Nez Perce
The Lakota Sioux
questions.explain: Miners flooded onto land guaranteed to the Lakota by the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie. Conflict followed, including the defeat of Custer at the Little Bighorn in 1876.

questions.q: What did Helen Hunt Jackson's 1881 book A Century of Dishonor seek to do?
options: Defend the sale of reservation land to railroads and settlers
Encourage farm families to migrate to the Plains
Expose broken federal promises to Native Americans
Praise the army's conduct on the Plains
questions.explain: Jackson documented treaty violations to shame the public into reform. Her work contributed to calls for changes in Indian policy.

questions.q: By the 1880s the bison herds of the Great Plains had been nearly destroyed. Which factor contributed most to this?
options: Competition for grass from Texas cattle drives
Commercial hide hunting made possible by railroads
Fencing of the open range with barbed wire
Severe droughts that dried up Plains rivers in the 1860s
questions.explain: Hide hunters shot bison in vast numbers, and the army and settlers welcomed the loss because it undermined the economic base of Plains nations.

questions.q: Which invention of the 1870s helped farmers and ranchers fence the treeless Plains cheaply?
options: The cotton gin
Barbed wire
The steel plow
The mechanical reaper
questions.explain: Joseph Glidden's barbed wire could enclose large areas without scarce timber. It helped end the open range and sparked conflicts over land use.

questions.q: The open-range cattle industry declined in the late 1880s mainly because of...
options: Harsh winters, overgrazing and fencing
A federal ban on beef exports
The collapse of the railroad network
The invention of canned beef
questions.explain: Blizzards in 1886 and 1887 killed huge herds, while barbed wire and overgrazed pastures made ranching on the open range less profitable.

questions.q: In 1883 American railroads adopted standard time zones primarily to...
options: Comply with a new federal law passed in 1883
End the confusion of many local times
Match Greenwich time in every town
Help telegraph companies sell more messages
questions.explain: Each town used its own sun time, which made timetables chaotic. Railroad companies introduced four zones, and the federal government made them law decades later.

questions.q: Which was a common criticism by farmers of railroads in the 1870s and 1880s?
options: Railroads were run by the federal government
Railroads refused to carry grain from small farms
Railroad companies sold their land grants only to foreign buyers
Rates were higher on short rural hauls than on competitive lines
questions.explain: Where one line had a monopoly, farmers paid steep rates. The Grange and later the Farmers' Alliance demanded regulation.

questions.q: What did the Supreme Court rule in Munn v. Illinois (1877)?
options: Congress alone could regulate grain storage
States could regulate businesses serving the public interest
Private businesses are exempt from regulation
The Fourteenth Amendment bars every state law about private business
questions.explain: The Court upheld Illinois regulation of grain elevators, a win for the Granger movement. Later rulings narrowed state power over interstate rates.

questions.q: The 1886 Wabash case, which curbed state regulation of interstate railroad rates, helped lead Congress to pass the...
options: Interstate Commerce Act
Pendleton Act
Dawes Act
Bland-Allison Act
questions.explain: When the Court said states could not set rates on traffic crossing state lines, pressure grew for national regulation, producing the 1887 law.

questions.q: In United States v. E.C. Knight (1895), the Supreme Court limited the Sherman Act by finding that...
options: The Sherman Act applied only to railroads
Manufacturing was not interstate commerce
The sugar trust controlled too little of the market to restrain trade
The Sherman Act violated freedom of contract under the Fourteenth Amendment
questions.explain: The Court allowed the sugar trust's control of refining to stand, reasoning that manufacturing came before commerce, which weakened antitrust enforcement.

questions.q: In re Debs (1895) upheld which action?
options: The court-ordered break-up of the Standard Oil Company in 1892
An eight-hour workday for all coal miners
A national ban on child labor in factories
A federal injunction against the Pullman boycott
questions.explain: The Court said the government could stop interference with interstate commerce and the mail, giving employers a powerful tool against strikes.

questions.q: Andrew Carnegie made his fortune mainly in which industry?
options: Steel
Oil
Railroads
Banking
questions.explain: Carnegie Steel used efficient new methods, and in 1901 Carnegie sold it to a group led by J.P. Morgan.

questions.q: John D. Rockefeller built his fortune in which industry?
options: Oil refining
Steel
Meatpacking
Textiles
questions.explain: Rockefeller's Standard Oil came to control most American refining by buying out or pressuring competitors.

questions.q: What is Carnegie's strategy of buying iron ore mines, coke ovens and railroads to control every step of production called?
options: Horizontal integration
Collective bargaining
Scientific management
Vertical integration
questions.explain: By owning suppliers and transport, Carnegie cut costs and avoided dependence on other firms. This differs from absorbing rival producers.

questions.q: Rockefeller's practice of buying out competing refineries to dominate one stage of an industry is called...
options: Vertical integration
Collective bargaining
Scientific management
Horizontal integration
questions.explain: By absorbing rivals in the same business, Standard Oil gained power over prices. Critics saw it as a monopoly that crushed small firms.

questions.q: Cornelius Vanderbilt and his heirs built wealth chiefly by consolidating which kind of business?
options: Steel mills in Pittsburgh
Railroads such as the New York Central
Oil refineries in Cleveland
Banking houses on Wall Street
questions.explain: Vanderbilt first built shipping fortunes, then merged lines into the New York Central system, a model of large-scale railroad consolidation.

questions.q: J. P. Morgan is associated with the Gilded Age economy chiefly as a...
options: A labor leader who organized the steelworkers of Pittsburgh in 1892
A financier who reorganized railroads and built giant firms
The inventor of the process for making cheap steel
A Populist candidate who ran for president in 1892
questions.explain: Morgan's bank raised capital and merged firms. In 1895 he helped the Treasury replenish gold reserves, and in 1901 he formed US Steel.

questions.q: In his essay "Wealth" (the Gospel of Wealth), Andrew Carnegie argued that rich people should...
options: Use their fortunes for society during their lifetimes
Leave nearly all their property to their children
Avoid giving to charity so the poor stay motivated
Hand all of their fortunes over to the national government
questions.explain: Carnegie believed wealth carried a duty. He funded thousands of public libraries and other institutions, while opposing indiscriminate charity.

questions.q: Social Darwinists such as William Graham Sumner claimed that...
options: Government should break up every large firm
All wealth ought to be divided equally among citizens
Churches should take control of the largest industries in each state
Competition and survival of the fittest explain inequality
questions.explain: Applying evolutionary ideas to society, Social Darwinists defended laissez-faire policies and opposed government aid to the poor.

questions.q: Herbert Spencer's ideas were used in the Gilded Age mainly to...
options: Argue for stronger regulation of trusts
Support Social Gospel reforms
Defend the Populist platform
Justify unregulated competition
questions.explain: Spencer coined "survival of the fittest" for society. Business leaders and some writers cited his theories to defend the wealth gap.

questions.q: The Social Gospel movement urged churches to...
options: Stay out of questions about industry and wages
Support the theory of Social Darwinism
Promote migration to the West for city families
Address poverty, slums and factory conditions
questions.explain: Ministers such as Washington Gladden argued that Christian faith demanded reform of unjust industrial conditions.

questions.q: Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner gave the era its name with which 1873 novel?
options: The Jungle
The Gilded Age
The Octopus
The Red Badge of Courage
questions.explain: The satire mocked greed and corruption in post-war America. A gilded surface looks golden but covers cheaper material.

questions.q: Which author wrote Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884-85), a work of Gilded Age realism?
options: Stephen Crane
Henry James
Edith Wharton
Mark Twain
questions.explain: Twain used regional speech and satire to portray the Mississippi River world and the cruelty of slavery, written in the decades after the Civil War.

questions.q: Literary realism in the late 1800s differed from earlier romanticism by...
options: Focusing on the heroic figures and battles of the nation's past
Celebrating the beauty of untouched wilderness
Stressing spiritual transformation and emotion
Depicting ordinary life and social problems plainly
questions.explain: Writers such as William Dean Howells and Stephen Crane portrayed everyday people and the harsh effects of city life and industry.

questions.q: Stephen Crane's Maggie: A Girl of the Streets (1893) is an example of writing about...
options: Frontier ranching
Plantation society
Slum life in New York City
Civil War battles
questions.explain: Crane's short novel shows poverty and its effects on a young woman, part of a wave of realist and naturalist fiction.

questions.q: Charlotte Perkins Gilman's story "The Yellow Wallpaper" (1892) criticized...
options: Child labor in the textile mills of New England and the South
Limits on immigration from Southern Europe
Medical and social restrictions placed on women
Political corruption in the big cities
questions.explain: Gilman drew on her own experience of a "rest cure" to attack the way women's mental health and independence were treated.

questions.q: Jacob Riis's 1890 book How the Other Half Lives used photographs and text to expose...
options: Crowded tenement conditions in New York City
Corruption among members of the Senate and the House
Child labor on Southern cotton farms
Dangers in the meatpacking industry
questions.explain: Riis showed middle-class readers the slums of immigrant neighborhoods, and his work contributed to later tenement reform.

questions.q: Hull House, founded in Chicago in 1889 by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr, was an example of...
options: The headquarters of a national labor union
A social club run by a city political machine for its voters
A boarding school for Native children
A settlement house serving immigrant neighborhoods
questions.explain: Settlement houses offered classes, childcare and social services, and their residents often pushed for city and state reforms.

questions.q: Between about 1900 and 1914, most immigrants to the United States came from...
options: Northern and Western Europe
Mexico and Central America
East Asia
Southern and Eastern Europe
questions.explain: Italians, Poles and Jews from Russian lands arrived in growing numbers. They often settled in cities and took industrial jobs.

questions.q: Which immigration station opened in New York Harbor in 1892?
options: Angel Island
Ellis Island
Liberty Island
Castle Garden
questions.explain: The federal government ran Ellis Island, where officials inspected arrivals. Millions of Europeans passed through it in later decades.

questions.q: The term "nativism" refers to...
options: Support for the sovereignty of tribal nations
A movement to return families to rural life
Hostility to immigrants by native-born residents
Opposition to American involvement in foreign wars
questions.explain: Nativists feared that newcomers, especially Catholics and Jews, threatened American culture and jobs. Groups such as the American Protective Association spread such views.

questions.q: Which Gilded Age monument, dedicated in 1886, became a symbol welcoming immigrants?
options: The Statue of Liberty
The Washington Monument
The Lincoln Memorial
The Brooklyn Bridge
questions.explain: A gift from France, the statue stood near Ellis Island. Emma Lazarus's poem, added to its pedestal in 1903, strengthened the welcoming image.

questions.q: The Knights of Labor, led by Terence Powderly, were unusual among 1880s unions because they...
options: Admitted only skilled craftsmen from a single trade
Excluded all immigrants and non-citizens from membership in local assemblies
Welcomed skilled and unskilled workers, including Black workers
Organized only locomotive engineers and conductors
questions.explain: The Knights sought to unite all producers. Their membership peaked in 1886 and then dropped after Haymarket and failed strikes.

questions.q: The American Federation of Labor, led by Samuel Gompers, mostly focused on...
options: Creating a socialist government to replace capitalism
Organizing every unskilled laborer into one big union
Forming a third political party to win the presidency
Higher wages, shorter hours and better conditions
questions.explain: Gompers favored "bread-and-butter" goals and bargaining with employers, building a durable federation of craft unions founded in 1886.

questions.q: The 1886 Haymarket affair in Chicago began as a rally in support of...
options: Abolition of child labor
The eight-hour workday
Government ownership of the railroads
A boycott of Pullman cars
questions.explain: A bomb exploded as police moved to disperse the meeting, killing police officers and civilians. Anarchists were convicted, and unions suffered from public fear.

questions.q: How did the Haymarket affair affect the labor movement?
options: It linked unions with violence and radicalism
It ended employer opposition to labor unions
It led Congress to pass a national eight-hour law
It made the Knights of Labor the nation's largest union
questions.explain: Public alarm after the bombing damaged the Knights of Labor and encouraged employers and courts to take harder lines against unions.

questions.q: The 1892 strike at Carnegie's Homestead steel mill ended with...
options: A national law guaranteeing collective bargaining rights to steelworkers
A compromise wage deal brokered by President Harrison
Defeat of the union after a clash with Pinkertons and the militia
Carnegie agreeing to a closed shop for all his mills
questions.explain: Henry Clay Frick locked out workers. Armed Pinkertons fought strikers, and the militia protected strikebreakers, crushing unionism in the steel industry for decades.

questions.q: The Pullman Strike of 1894 began after the Pullman Company...
options: Required all workers to join a company-run union
Lengthened the workday to twelve hours
Closed its Illinois plant permanently
Cut wages without lowering rents in its company town
questions.explain: Workers appealed to Eugene Debs's American Railway Union, which launched a boycott of Pullman cars and disrupted rail traffic across the nation.

questions.q: President Grover Cleveland's response to the Pullman Strike was to...
options: Negotiate a settlement directly with Eugene Debs
Propose that the government take over the railroads
Obtain an injunction and send troops to keep trains running
Publicly support the strikers' demands for higher pay and lower rents
questions.explain: The federal government acted to protect the mail and interstate commerce. Debs was jailed, and the use of injunctions against strikes became a common weapon.

questions.q: President Rutherford B. Hayes used federal troops in 1877 to help end which event?
options: The Pullman Strike
The Haymarket affair
The Great Railroad Strike
The Homestead Strike
questions.explain: A wave of strikes after railroad wage cuts spread from West Virginia across the country. It was the first nationwide strike and was ended with force.

questions.q: The Supreme Court in Williams v. Mississippi (1898) allowed...
options: Voting restrictions that were race-neutral on their face
A federal ban on the use of literacy tests
The right of Black candidates to run in Southern primaries
Federal supervision of elections across the South
questions.explain: Because the law did not mention race, the Court let it stand, even though it was administered to exclude Black voters.

questions.q: What did the Supreme Court hold in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)?
options: Segregation in public schools was unlawful
Railroads were not allowed to carry both races in the same train
Segregated facilities were legal if "separate but equal"
Louisiana's law violated the Thirteenth Amendment
questions.explain: Homer Plessy challenged Louisiana's railcar law. The ruling gave legal cover to Jim Crow for nearly 60 years, with only Justice Harlan dissenting.

questions.q: What did Justice John Marshall Harlan's lone dissent in Plessy argue?
options: Segregation should be extended to public schools in every state
States had no power at all over railroad cars
The Constitution is color-blind, so the law was unconstitutional
Plessy lacked standing to bring the case
questions.explain: Harlan warned that the ruling would stimulate racial aggression and violate equal rights, a view later cited by opponents of segregation.

questions.q: What is the set of state and local laws that enforced racial segregation in the South known as?
options: Jim Crow laws
The Black Codes of 1866
The Freedmen's laws
The Redeemer treaties
questions.explain: Jim Crow laws separated Black and white Americans in schools, transport and public places, supported by the threat of violence.

questions.q: Ida B. Wells became nationally known in the 1890s for...
options: Investigating and condemning lynching
Founding the Tuskegee Institute in rural Alabama
Leading the Populist Party
Directing the Freedmen's Bureau
questions.explain: After the lynching of friends in Memphis in 1892, Wells wrote and spoke about it, publishing Southern Horrors and traveling internationally.

questions.q: Booker T. Washington's Atlanta Exposition address of 1895 urged Black Americans to...
options: Focus on economic progress and vocational training while accepting segregation
Demand immediate and full political equality at the ballot box and in the courts
Emigrate to Africa and build a new nation there
Boycott Southern industry until segregation ended
questions.explain: Often called the Atlanta Compromise, the speech won praise from white leaders but criticism from those who thought it gave up on civil rights.

questions.q: Booker T. Washington headed which institution founded in Alabama in 1881?
options: Tuskegee Institute
Howard University
Fisk University
Atlanta University
questions.explain: Tuskegee taught trades and teaching skills. Washington believed economic independence would earn respect.

questions.q: How did W.E.B. Du Bois differ from Booker T. Washington?
options: He opposed the schooling of Black students beyond grade school level
He demanded civil rights and college education for a "Talented Tenth"
He urged Black Americans to accept segregation in the South
He supported only vocational training for Black students
questions.explain: Du Bois argued that political rights and college-educated leaders were essential. He later helped found the Niagara Movement and the NAACP.

questions.q: The 1898 events in Wilmington, North Carolina, in which an armed white mob overthrew the elected local government, show...
options: How violence was used to end Black political participation in a city
The success of Populist-led voting reforms across the South
Federal protection of local elections in the Carolinas
The spread of the Knights of Labor in Southern ports
questions.explain: After a campaign of white supremacy, a mob destroyed a Black newspaper and forced officials from office, with many killed.

questions.q: Farmers in the 1890s often supported "free silver" because they believed it would...
options: Increase the money supply and raise crop prices
Make loans harder to get and lower the cost of farm tools
Lower tariffs on imports and farm tools
Cut federal spending and the national debt
questions.explain: Falling prices left farmers struggling with debts. More silver money, they hoped, would cause inflation and ease repayment.

questions.q: Supporters of the gold standard argued that it would...
options: Raise farm prices through added coinage of silver dollars
Encourage inflation to ease debts
Replace private banks with federal ones
Keep the currency stable and protect investors
questions.explain: Bankers and creditors feared silver coinage would weaken the dollar. Debate over money dominated the 1890s.

questions.q: The Bland-Allison Act of 1878, passed over President Hayes's veto, required the Treasury to...
options: Stop the printing of all paper money
Buy a set amount of silver each month and coin it
Issue gold certificates and no other form of paper currency
Withdraw all greenbacks from circulation
questions.explain: It was a compromise that satisfied silver supporters only partly. Treasury purchases were limited and the gold standard stayed in place.

questions.q: The Sherman Silver Purchase Act of 1890 contributed to the Panic of 1893 because it...
options: Drained the Treasury's gold reserve as notes were redeemed
Stopped silver mining across the Western states
Raised tariffs to the highest level in the nation's history
Allowed banks to hold no reserves at all
questions.explain: The Treasury paid for silver with notes redeemable in coin, and holders mostly demanded gold. Falling gold reserves alarmed investors and helped trigger the Panic of 1893.

questions.q: President Cleveland asked Congress in 1893 to repeal the Sherman Silver Purchase Act in order to...
options: Raise the market price of silver for the Western mining states
Help farmers by encouraging mild inflation
Protect the gold reserve and confidence in the dollar
Lower the national debt by raising a tariff
questions.explain: Repeal split his Democratic Party and angered silver supporters in the South and West, who turned toward Bryan in 1896.

questions.q: The Populist (People's) Party's Omaha Platform of 1892 called for...
options: A return to the gold standard and a high tariff
Repeal of the Homestead Act and an end to railroad land grants
Private ownership of the railroads and telegraph lines
A graduated income tax and direct election of senators
questions.explain: Populists also wanted government ownership of railroads, free coinage of silver and the secret ballot. Many demands later became law.

questions.q: Which Populist demand was fulfilled by the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913?
options: The graduated income tax on large incomes
The secret ballot
Direct election of US senators
Free coinage of silver
questions.explain: Before 1913, state legislatures picked senators. Reformers argued that this allowed wealthy interests to buy seats.

questions.q: The Supreme Court struck down the 1894 income tax in Pollock v. Farmers' Loan and Trust (1895) by calling it...
options: An unconstitutional direct tax
An improper tariff
An unconstitutional export duty
A tax on interstate commerce
questions.explain: Populists and reformers later won the Sixteenth Amendment in 1913 to authorize an income tax without apportionment.

questions.q: William Jennings Bryan's "Cross of Gold" speech of 1896 was a defense of...
options: Free coinage of silver and working farmers
The gold standard and Eastern bankers
A high protective tariff for Northern manufacturers and steel firms
Imperial expansion into the Pacific
questions.explain: Bryan told the Democratic convention that the nation should not crucify mankind on a cross of gold. The speech won him the nomination.

questions.q: The 1896 presidential election between William McKinley and William Jennings Bryan is considered a turning point because...
options: Republicans built a lasting majority of business and urban voters
Populists captured the White House for the first time in history
Silver replaced gold as the national currency
The House of Representatives decided the election
questions.explain: McKinley, managed by Mark Hanna, raised huge funds and won industrial states. The gold standard was later confirmed by law in 1900.

questions.q: Which man managed William McKinley's 1896 campaign and raised enormous sums from business?
options: Thomas Reed
Roscoe Conkling
James G. Blaine
Mark Hanna
questions.explain: Hanna's campaigning and fundraising set a pattern for modern campaigns. The Republican victory ended a decade of close elections.

questions.q: The 1888 election was unusual because Benjamin Harrison...
options: Won the presidency despite losing the popular vote
Won without carrying a single Northern state
Was elected by a vote in the House
Defeated a Populist candidate for the presidency in a close race
questions.explain: Grover Cleveland won more popular votes but lost the electoral college, and Harrison served one term before Cleveland returned in 1893.

questions.q: Grover Cleveland was the first president who...
options: Was elected president without belonging to any political party
Served as a Union general
Won a term as a Populist
Served two non-consecutive terms
questions.explain: He lost to Benjamin Harrison in 1888 and defeated him in 1892, so he is counted as both the 22nd and 24th president. Donald Trump, the 45th and 47th president, later became the second.

questions.q: House Speaker Thomas B. Reed changed House procedure in 1890 by...
options: Ending debate by majority vote of the Senate
Letting committees pass bills without any vote on the floor
Banning amendments in every case
Counting members present but not voting toward a quorum
questions.explain: Reed's rule stopped the minority from blocking action by refusing to answer roll calls. His critics nicknamed him "Czar Reed."

questions.q: The McKinley Tariff of 1890 did what?
options: Raised duties on many imports to high levels
Abolished all duties on imported goods
Created the first federal income tax
Lowered rates on imported cloth, iron and many other goods
questions.explain: Backed by Republicans to protect industry, it contributed to higher consumer prices, and voters punished the party in the 1890 elections.

questions.q: Jacob Coxey's "Army" arrived in Washington in 1894 to demand...
options: Free silver and the end of the gold standard for the dollar
Federal public works jobs for the unemployed
A ban on immigration
Land for homesteaders
questions.explain: During the depression, Coxey's march of jobless men ended at the Capitol, where he was arrested for walking on the grass.

questions.q: In the 1884 election, the Mugwumps were Republicans who...
options: Joined the Populists in the Midwest and the West that year
Left their party to back Democrat Grover Cleveland over Blaine
Strongly backed Blaine's tariff plan
Supported the Greenback Party for president
questions.explain: Reformers distrusted Blaine's reputation for corruption. Their defection helped narrowly elect Cleveland in New York and the nation.

questions.q: Before the Seventeenth Amendment, how did most senators get their seats?
options: Elected by a vote of the House
Chosen by their state legislatures
Appointed by the president
Selected by their state governors alone
questions.explain: Critics said this system encouraged bribery and made some Senate seats look like prizes for rich men.

questions.q: The Electoral Count Act of 1887 was passed in response to which crisis?
options: The Panic of 1873
The Pullman Strike
The disputed election of 1876
The Haymarket affair
questions.explain: Congress created procedures for resolving disputes over electoral votes so that another crisis like the Hayes-Tilden dispute would be less likely.

questions.q: Frederick Law Olmsted is connected to the US Capitol because he...
options: Painted the Rotunda's dome
Drew the plans for the Library of Congress and its reading room
Designed the landscape of the Capitol grounds
Sculpted the Statue of Freedom
questions.explain: After designing New York's Central Park, Olmsted laid out the Capitol's terraces and grounds beginning in the 1870s.

questions.q: The Jefferson Building of the Library of Congress, opened in 1897, is notable for...
options: Its use as the first home of the Supreme Court
Its design by Capitol architect Thomas U. Walter
Being the first federal building in Washington topped by a dome
Its lavish decoration by American artists and sculptors
questions.explain: It was built to hold a growing collection and became a symbol of national cultural ambition during the Gilded Age.

questions.q: The 1870 law that centralized US copyright registration in the Library of Congress also...
options: Limited copyright to ten years
Required deposit of copies of copyrighted works at the Library
Extended copyright to foreign authors
Created the separate Copyright Office
questions.explain: The deposit requirement helped build the Library's collections as authors registered books, maps, music and photographs.

questions.q: Thomas Edison's Menlo Park laboratory is famous for...
options: Inventing the telephone and building its first long-distance lines
Producing a practical electric light bulb in 1879
Building the first powered airplane
Perfecting the Bessemer steel process
questions.explain: Edison's team tested thousands of materials. He also developed a system of power generation and distribution, opening the Pearl Street Station in 1882.

questions.q: Alexander Graham Bell is credited with which invention patented in 1876?
options: The telephone
The telegraph
The phonograph
The typewriter
questions.explain: The telephone transformed communication and grew into a major national business under Bell's company.

questions.q: The Bessemer process made it possible to...
options: Produce steel cheaply in large quantities
Print newspapers at much higher speeds on rotary presses
Preserve meat on long railroad trips
Refine kerosene from crude oil
questions.explain: Cheap steel supported rails, bridges, skyscrapers and machines, driving the rise of firms like Carnegie Steel.

questions.q: Which structural development made skyscrapers possible in the 1880s and 1890s?
options: Steel frames and safe passenger elevators
Cast-iron facades and gas lighting
Load-bearing stone walls and iron stairways
Reinforced concrete and steam heating
questions.explain: Chicago architects such as Louis Sullivan used the steel skeleton to build tall office buildings in crowded downtown areas.

questions.q: Mail-order catalogs such as Montgomery Ward and Sears, Roebuck helped by...
options: Replacing the farm cooperatives of the Grange with national stores
Ending the use of cash in farm trade across the Midwest
Bringing manufactured goods to rural customers by rail and mail
Banning small local stores in towns across the country
questions.explain: Railroads and rural mail delivery let farm families order products from cities, creating a national consumer market.

questions.q: Department stores like Macy's and Marshall Field's reflected which Gilded Age trend?
options: The decline of fixed prices as bargaining returned
The growth of mass consumption in cities
The shift of most shopping to rural general stores
The end of credit and installment buying
questions.explain: Large stores offered many goods under one roof with fixed prices and displays, targeting middle-class shoppers.

questions.q: The 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago showcased...
options: Only agricultural products and machines from the Midwest farm states
Weapons and military equipment for the armed forces of the United States
New technology and an idealized "White City" of grand buildings
Native crafts, dances and villages from the Plains tribes only
questions.explain: The fair drew millions and influenced city planning. Its displays also reflected racial hierarchies of the time.

questions.q: Edward Bellamy's novel Looking Backward (1888) imagined...
options: A world dominated by powerful private monopolies
A new American empire in the Pacific
A peaceful, cooperative society in the year 2000
A return to farm life across the Midwest
questions.explain: The book's popularity inspired Nationalist clubs and influenced critics of industrial capitalism.

questions.q: What did Henry George's Progress and Poverty (1879) argue?
options: A single tax on land values could reduce inequality
All money should be backed by gold alone
Labor unions should be banned by law
Trusts should be allowed to run the nation's railroads
questions.explain: George claimed that rising land values enriched owners without effort. His ideas influenced reformers in cities and in later movements.

questions.q: Yellowstone, established in 1872, was the first...
options: Forest reserve
National park in the United States
Wildlife refuge
National monument in the United States, set aside by Congress
questions.explain: Congress set aside the area in Wyoming and neighboring territories, starting a conservation movement that later grew under Roosevelt.

questions.q: John Muir founded which conservation group in 1892?
options: The Audubon Society
The Wilderness Society
The Boone and Crockett Club
The Sierra Club
questions.explain: Muir championed the preservation of wilderness, in contrast to Gifford Pinchot's view that forests should be managed for use.

questions.q: The 1891 Forest Reserve Act (Harrison) allowed the president to...
options: Set aside forest land as protected public reserves
Open all forests to homesteaders under the Homestead Act
Transfer public forests to the states
Sell timber rights on public forests to railroads
questions.explain: It laid the foundation for national forests, which later expanded greatly under Theodore Roosevelt.

questions.q: The 1889 Oklahoma land run was...
options: A treaty negotiated with the Cherokee Nation over its western lands
A race by settlers to claim former Indian Territory lands
A railroad publicity stunt that promoted tickets to the Texas plains
A gold rush that sent prospectors into the Black Hills of Dakota
questions.explain: At noon on April 22, thousands rushed in to stake claims. Those who sneaked in early were called "Sooners."

questions.q: What did Frederick Jackson Turner's 1893 "frontier thesis" argue?
options: Immigration weakened the American character
Cities caused almost all democratic change
Slavery drove westward expansion
The frontier shaped American democracy
questions.explain: Turner built on the Census Bureau's 1890 statement that a continuous frontier line no longer existed. Later historians criticized his neglect of Native peoples.

questions.q: In 1890 the Census Bureau declared what about the frontier?
options: It was being closed by federal law
It had advanced to the Pacific coast for the first time
It had stalled at the Mississippi River
It no longer existed as a clear line of settlement
questions.explain: The announcement led Americans like Turner to reflect on the closing of the frontier and to look overseas for expansion.

questions.q: Farmers' Granges, founded in 1867, began as...
options: A group for rural social life that later pushed for regulation
A national political party that nominated candidates for president
A labor union for coal miners and iron and steel workers
A secret society of Southern landowners opposed to Reconstruction
questions.explain: Granges built cooperatives and backed Granger laws against railroad abuses. Later the Farmers' Alliance took up the cause more radically.

questions.q: What did the Farmers' Alliance's subtreasury plan propose?
options: Banks end all loans to farmers and rely only on cash sales
Railroads carry farm crops to market at no charge
The government store crops and lend money against them
Farmers pay no taxes on their land or machinery
questions.explain: Charles Macune's plan would have eased credit and avoided forced sales at harvest-time prices. Congress did not pass it, but it influenced Populism.

questions.q: The main cause of farmers' economic troubles in the late 1800s was...
options: Falling crop prices combined with debt and high transport costs
Overly cheap land that was free to anyone who asked for it
A shortage of railroads in the farming states of the Midwest
Strong overseas demand for grain that pushed prices up too fast
questions.explain: Global competition and overproduction pushed prices down, while fixed debts and rates made payments harder.

questions.q: The Women's Christian Temperance Union, led by Frances Willard, campaigned to...
options: Ban immigration from Eastern Europe
Reduce alcohol use and expand women's public role
Limit child labor in textile mills and coal mines only
Establish a national church for women
questions.explain: The WCTU linked temperance to home protection and later supported suffrage and other reforms.

questions.q: In 1890 the two major women's suffrage groups merged to form the...
options: National Woman's Party, led by Alice Paul in 1913
National American Woman Suffrage Association
League of Women Voters of 1920
Women's Trade Union League
questions.explain: Led by figures such as Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony, the unified group focused on winning state-by-state victories and a constitutional amendment.

questions.q: In 1869, which Western territory became the first place in the United States to grant women a lasting right to vote?
options: California
Texas
Montana
Wyoming Territory
questions.explain: Wyoming Territory took the step and kept it as a state in 1890. Several other Western states followed before the Nineteenth Amendment.

questions.q: What did Alfred Thayer Mahan's The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890) argue?
options: The United States should avoid foreign trade altogether and stay at home
Large land armies decided the balance of world power
A strong navy and overseas bases were vital to national power
Steam-powered ships had made navies obsolete
questions.explain: His book influenced American leaders such as Theodore Roosevelt and helped inspire naval expansion and imperial ambitions.

questions.q: In 1893 American planters in Hawaii, backed by US Marines, overthrew which ruler?
options: Queen Liliuokalani
King Kalakaua
Kamehameha III
Queen Emma
questions.explain: Sugar interests wanted annexation. President Cleveland opposed the overthrow, but Congress annexed Hawaii in 1898 during the Spanish-American War.

questions.q: The "yellow press" of William Randolph Hearst and Joseph Pulitzer helped push the nation toward war with Spain by...
options: Refusing to print any news about Cuba
Defending Spain's colonial policies
Banning political cartoons and all pictures from their pages
Printing sensational stories about Spanish rule in Cuba
questions.explain: Fierce competition for readers led to exaggerated reports of Spanish cruelty. The press did not cause the war alone but intensified public pressure.

questions.q: Which slogan did the American press and public adopt after the USS Maine exploded in Havana Harbor in 1898?
options: Remember the Maine!
Don't give up the ship!
Fifty-four forty or fight!
Remember the Alamo!
questions.explain: The cause of the explosion was never settled to everyone's satisfaction at the time, but the press blamed Spain, and the cry 'Remember the Maine!' helped push the nation toward war.

questions.q: The main mast of the USS Maine is now displayed at which Washington-area site?
options: Mount Vernon
Arlington National Cemetery
The Armed Forces Retirement Home
Fort McNair
questions.explain: Many of the sailors killed in 1898 were buried in Arlington, and the mast stands there as a memorial to them.

questions.q: The Teller Amendment of 1898 stated that the United States would...
options: Annex Cuba
Not annex Cuba after the war
Buy Cuba from Spain
Withdraw from the Philippines
questions.explain: Congress's resolution for war said the US had no intention of ruling Cuba, though later arrangements, such as the Platt Amendment, gave it influence.

questions.q: On May 1, 1898, Commodore George Dewey destroyed the Spanish fleet in...
options: Santiago Harbor in Cuba
Havana Harbor
Manila Bay in the Philippines
San Juan Bay
questions.explain: The victory, achieved with little American loss, led to an American occupation of Manila and growing interest in keeping the islands.

questions.q: Which unit led by Theodore Roosevelt and Leonard Wood became famous for fighting in Cuba in 1898?
options: The Green Mountain Boys
Berdan's Sharpshooters
The Flying Tigers
The Rough Riders
questions.explain: The volunteer cavalry fought at Kettle Hill and San Juan Heights, helping make Roosevelt a national hero. Black regular regiments also fought there.

questions.q: Which units of Black soldiers fought with distinction at San Juan Hill in 1898?
options: The 9th and 10th Cavalry (Buffalo Soldiers)
The 54th Massachusetts Volunteer Infantry of the Civil War
The Tuskegee Airmen's fighter group
The 92nd Infantry Division
questions.explain: Black regulars of the Army served in the war, and several earned medals despite discrimination in the army.

questions.q: Under the 1898 Treaty of Paris ending the Spanish-American War, Spain ceded the Philippines, Guam and...
options: Puerto Rico
Hawaii
Jamaica
Panama
questions.explain: The treaty gave the US an overseas empire. Spain gave up Cuba, and the US paid Spain $20 million for the Philippines.

questions.q: The Senate vote on the Treaty of Paris in 1899 was very close mainly because...
options: Anti-imperialists opposed taking the Philippines
Southern senators wanted Cuba annexed
Senators demanded that Spain be paid more
Many senators wanted Hawaii returned to its queen
questions.explain: Two-thirds were needed, and the treaty passed 57-27 on February 6, 1899, with just one vote to spare after intense debate over whether the nation should hold colonies.

questions.q: Which group, including Mark Twain and Andrew Carnegie, opposed American annexation of the Philippines?
options: The Navy League
The American Colonization Society
The Anti-Imperialist League
The Grange
questions.explain: Members argued that ruling people without consent contradicted American principles of self-government.

questions.q: The Philippine-American War (1899-1902) began when Filipino nationalists led by Emilio Aguinaldo...
options: Invaded Guam after the treaty
Resisted American rule after expecting independence
Demanded statehood for the islands
Allied with Spain to defend the islands
questions.explain: Filipinos who had fought Spain turned against the new colonial power. The war was long and harsh, with many civilian deaths.

questions.q: Why did many business leaders and politicians in the 1890s urge the United States to acquire overseas markets?
options: They sought to replace the gold standard with silver
They wanted to relieve a national shortage of cotton and wheat
They hoped to reduce immigration to American cities
They feared American farms and factories were producing more than Americans could buy
questions.explain: After the Panic of 1893, many leaders blamed overproduction and argued that foreign markets would ease depressions, which helped build support for imperial moves.

questions.q: What did Josiah Strong's 1885 book Our Country argue?
options: Anglo-Saxon Protestants had a mission to spread civilization
America should withdraw all of its missionaries
Immigration would strengthen American democracy
The frontier was closing and Americans should look only inward
questions.explain: The book combined religious zeal with racial theories and helped build support for expansion overseas.

questions.q: What did Booker T. Washington's National Negro Business League, founded in 1900, promote?
options: Black-owned enterprise as a path to security under Jim Crow
Federal civil rights legislation passed by Congress that year
Mass strikes against Southern employers
Mass migration of Black families to Africa
questions.explain: Washington promoted self-help and business ownership. Critics such as Du Bois thought this approach gave too little weight to political rights.

questions.q: Why did railroads employ the practice of "rebates" in the Gilded Age?
options: To give favored large shippers secret discounts
To pay farmers for letting tracks cross their land
To refund the fares of unhappy passengers
To subsidize the building of canals
questions.explain: Rebates helped giants like Standard Oil beat smaller rivals, and farmers and small shippers resented the discrimination.

questions.q: Why did big-city political machines often gain loyalty from immigrants?
options: They offered jobs, services and help in exchange for votes
They banned nativist groups from city politics
They gave immigrants federal land grants
They protected immigrants from deportation under federal law
questions.explain: Machine bosses provided services that city governments lacked. Reformers criticized the graft that came with the system.

questions.q: The "New South" idea of leaders like Henry Grady promoted...
options: A return to plantation farming and cotton as the only crop
Industrialization such as textile mills and steel
A ban on railroad building in the region
Federal ownership of Southern farmland
questions.explain: Many Southern towns grew, but wages stayed low and most of the region remained poor and dependent on cotton.

questions.q: The "crop-lien system" in the post-Civil War South tied farmers to...
options: Federal land offices that sold small farms to freed people
Merchants who gave supplies on credit against future crops
Railroad companies that shipped the cotton
Agents of the Freedmen's Bureau
questions.explain: High interest and the push to grow cotton left families in debt year after year, making them dependent on the merchant.

questions.q: The Pendleton Act initially covered about 10 percent of federal jobs but became a lasting reform partly because...
options: It passed Congress unanimously
It banned all patronage from the start
Presidents could extend the classified list
It applied to elected offices
questions.explain: Later presidents widened coverage, so more jobs depended on merit.

questions.q: What did Frederick Winslow Taylor's "scientific management" in the 1890s and 1900s aim to do?
options: Increase factory efficiency through time-and-motion study
Raise the wages of factory workers through federal legislation
Move factory workers back to the farms to cut city crowding
Break up large trusts by order of federal courts
questions.explain: Taylor's methods were criticized by workers as speedups. They influenced later ideas such as the assembly line.

questions.q: Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle (1906) shocked readers by describing conditions in which industry?
options: Coal mining
Meatpacking
Textile manufacturing
Railroad building
questions.explain: Sinclair meant to expose immigrant workers' suffering, but readers reacted most to the unsanitary food, which pushed Congress to act.

questions.q: The Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906 were passed after...
options: A Supreme Court order that required inspection of all food
A Populist election victory that gave the party control of Congress
A national strike organized by the AFL against meatpackers
Muckraking exposés and pressure from President Theodore Roosevelt
questions.explain: Public outrage over The Jungle and other reports helped create federal inspection and labeling rules, expanding the government's role in consumer safety.

questions.q: Journalists such as Ida Tarbell and Lincoln Steffens, who exposed corruption and abuses, were called...
options: Muckrakers
Mugwumps
Stalwarts
Populists
questions.explain: President Roosevelt popularized the term in 1906. Tarbell investigated Standard Oil in McClure's Magazine, and Steffens wrote about city machines.

questions.q: Lincoln Steffens's The Shame of the Cities (1904) mainly exposed...
options: Unsafe conditions in meatpacking
Child labor in Southern mills
Corruption in municipal government
Unfair practices of Standard Oil
questions.explain: Steffens reported on bosses and business leaders who cooperated in big cities, strengthening support for municipal reform.

questions.q: Ida Tarbell's series on Standard Oil, published in McClure's, criticized the company for...
options: Hiring only child laborers to cut the company's costs
Poisoning rivers with refinery waste near Cleveland
Using unfair tactics to crush competitors
Selling spoiled meat to the army during the war
questions.explain: Tarbell's careful research of Rockefeller's methods influenced public opinion before the government broke up the company in 1911.

questions.q: What did Theodore Roosevelt's "Square Deal" aim to do?
options: End all federal regulation of business and leave markets alone
Support only the interests of the largest businesses
Treat capital, labor and the public fairly through government
Break up every labor union and ban strikes by law
questions.explain: Roosevelt described his program with the phrase, and it covered controlling trusts, protecting consumers and conserving resources.

questions.q: President Roosevelt's response to the 1902 anthracite coal strike was unusual because he...
options: Sent federal troops to the coalfields to end the strike
Ignored the strike as a private matter between the parties
Acted as a mediator rather than siding with the owners
Banned the miners' union by executive order
questions.explain: The government pressed both sides toward arbitration, and miners received a pay raise and shorter hours, though the union was not formally recognized.

questions.q: The Supreme Court's 1904 Northern Securities decision upheld the...
options: The government's power to set railroad rates
Breakup of a railroad holding company under the Sherman Act
Dissolution of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey
The right of railroad workers to organize
questions.explain: The ruling helped earn Roosevelt a reputation as a "trust buster," though he distinguished "good" and "bad" trusts.

questions.q: The Hepburn Act of 1906 strengthened which agency?
options: The Forest Service
The Federal Reserve
The Federal Trade Commission
The Interstate Commerce Commission
questions.explain: It gave the ICC power to set maximum railroad rates, a major step in federal regulation.

questions.q: Which Roosevelt-era law allowed presidents to protect sites like Devils Tower as national monuments?
options: The Antiquities Act of 1906
The Newlands Act
The Forest Reserve Act
The Homestead Act
questions.explain: Presidents have used the law to proclaim many monuments without waiting for Congress.

questions.q: Gifford Pinchot, head of the US Forest Service, believed that forests should be...
options: Left completely untouched by lumber and mining firms
Sold to private owners
Managed wisely for sustained use
Cleared for farms
questions.explain: His utilitarian conservation differed from John Muir's preservationist views. Roosevelt backed Pinchot while adding millions of acres to national forests.

questions.q: The Hetch Hetchy controversy of the 1900s and 1910s pitted preservationists against supporters of...
options: Mining for gold inside the boundaries of Yellowstone National Park
Damming a Yosemite valley to supply water to San Francisco
Logging the forests of Alaska for the lumber trade
Draining the swamps of the Everglades for farmland
questions.explain: Congress approved the dam in 1913, a defeat for John Muir and the Sierra Club that helped sharpen the debate over conservation.

questions.q: The National Park Service was created in 1916 under President...
options: Woodrow Wilson
Theodore Roosevelt
William Taft
Warren Harding
questions.explain: Congress established the agency to manage parks "unimpaired" for future generations.

questions.q: The Newlands Reclamation Act of 1902 funded...
options: Irrigation projects in arid Western states
Rural free delivery of the mail
Railroad bridges across the great Western rivers
New national forests in the Rockies
questions.explain: Money from public land sales built dams and canals, which transformed Western farming and also changed rivers and landscapes.

questions.q: William Howard Taft is the only person to have served as...
options: Speaker of the House and President of the United States
Vice President and Chief Justice of the United States
President and Chief Justice of the United States
Senator and Secretary of State of the United States
questions.explain: After leaving the presidency in 1913, he became Chief Justice in 1921 and led the Court for most of the 1920s.

questions.q: Before the Supreme Court's own building opened in 1935, where did the Court meet?
options: In the Library of Congress
In the old Executive Office Building
In the Capitol
In the Department of Justice building
questions.explain: Chief Justice Taft pushed Congress to fund a separate building, which Cass Gilbert designed. Taft died in 1930 and the Court moved in during 1935.

questions.q: President Taft's administration is known for which antitrust action?
options: The 1911 breakup of Standard Oil
The 1890 passage of the Sherman Act
The 1904 breakup of the Northern Securities Company
The 1901 creation of US Steel
questions.explain: The Supreme Court ordered Standard Oil split into separate companies in 1911, applying a "rule of reason" to the Sherman Act.

questions.q: The Sixteenth Amendment, ratified in 1913, authorized Congress to...
options: Elect US senators directly by popular vote of the people
Ban the sale of alcoholic beverages across the nation
Levy an income tax without apportioning it among states
Allow women to vote in all federal elections
questions.explain: The amendment overcame the Pollock decision. It created a new source of federal revenue and later paid for wars and social programs.

questions.q: The Seventeenth Amendment, ratified in 1913, changed the way that...
options: Presidents are inaugurated
Senators are chosen, by direct popular vote
The Supreme Court is appointed
Representatives are apportioned among the states by census
questions.explain: Progressives believed direct election would reduce corruption and make the Senate more responsive to the public.

questions.q: The Eighteenth Amendment, ratified in 1919, did what?
options: Gave women the right to vote in all federal elections
Created the first permanent federal income tax
Prohibited making and selling alcoholic beverages
Limited the president to two terms in office
questions.explain: Temperance groups and Progressives had campaigned for decades. Enforcement came through the Volstead Act, and the amendment was repealed in 1933.

questions.q: The Nineteenth Amendment, certified in August 1920, guaranteed...
options: Direct election of senators by the voters of each state
An income tax
Prohibition
The right to vote regardless of sex
questions.explain: After a long struggle, Tennessee provided the 36th state ratification. Many women of color still faced barriers at the polls.

questions.q: The "Silent Sentinels," who picketed the White House in 1917, were members of which group?
options: The WCTU
The Anti-Saloon League
The National Woman's Party
The Women's Trade Union League
questions.explain: Led by Alice Paul, they held banners addressed to President Wilson. Many were arrested, and some endured harsh treatment and hunger strikes.

questions.q: Carrie Chapman Catt's strategy for NAWSA, in contrast with the National Woman's Party, was to...
options: Press for state victories and a federal amendment while backing the war
Hold picket lines outside the White House gates every day
Boycott elections until women were allowed to vote
Seek a new constitutional convention to rewrite the whole Constitution
questions.explain: Catt's "Winning Plan" mixed state campaigns with pressure on Congress. The two approaches together helped push passage in 1919.

questions.q: Which two women's rights pioneers' statues are among those in the Portrait Monument given to the Capitol in 1921?
options: Lucy Stone and Julia Ward Howe
Sojourner Truth and Harriet Tubman
Alice Paul and Carrie Chapman Catt
Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony
questions.explain: The sculpture by Adelaide Johnson also shows Lucretia Mott. It honors pioneers of the suffrage movement and stands in the Capitol.

questions.q: The 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York City led to calls for reform because...
options: The factory was the largest clothing factory in the nation
It destroyed an immigrant neighborhood
Locked exits contributed to the deaths of 146 workers
It occurred during a strike
questions.explain: Most victims were young immigrant women. The disaster spurred state fire codes and labor legislation, with Frances Perkins among the reformers.

questions.q: In Lochner v. New York (1905), the Supreme Court struck down a law limiting bakers' hours by reasoning that...
options: It violated "liberty of contract" under the Fourteenth Amendment
Bakers were not employees under the terms of the state law
Only Congress could regulate working hours for any worker
Baking was a form of interstate commerce under the Constitution
questions.explain: The decision symbolized judicial resistance to labor regulation, and the Court later moved away from it in the 1930s.

questions.q: In Muller v. Oregon (1908), the Court upheld a limit on women's working hours after hearing...
options: Social science evidence in a brief by Louis Brandeis
Testimony from factory owners and union leaders in court
An argument based on a treaty with a foreign power
Testimony from members of Congress about women workers
questions.explain: The Brandeis brief gathered data on health effects. The ruling relied on assumptions about women that later reformers challenged.

questions.q: In Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918), the Supreme Court struck down a federal law about...
options: Sedition and criticism of the war effort by newspapers
Child labor in goods shipped across state lines
Railroad rates and rebates in interstate commerce
The collection of the new federal income tax
questions.explain: The Court held that Congress overreached its commerce power. A later Court overruled it in 1941 when it upheld the Fair Labor Standards Act.

questions.q: In Adkins v. Children's Hospital (1923), a case from the District of Columbia, the Supreme Court ruled that...
options: A maximum workday for District women was invalid
A minimum wage law for women violated freedom of contract
A federal child labor tax was unconstitutional
Congress could not tax the income of District residents
questions.explain: The decision was overruled in 1937 by West Coast Hotel v. Parrish, which upheld a state minimum wage.

questions.q: In 1937 the Supreme Court's decision in West Coast Hotel v. Parrish was seen as significant because it...
options: Upheld a state minimum wage law and signaled acceptance of regulation
Struck down Social Security as an unconstitutional federal program
Ended the New Deal in a series of Supreme Court rulings
Banned labor unions from the workplace in every state
questions.explain: Many observers called it the "switch in time that saved nine," since it came while FDR's Court-packing plan was pending.

questions.q: In the 1912 presidential election, Theodore Roosevelt ran as the candidate of which party?
options: The Progressive ("Bull Moose") Party
The Socialist Party led by Eugene V. Debs
The Prohibition Party led by temperance reformers
The Populist Party of the 1890s
questions.explain: Roosevelt split the Republican vote with Taft, helping Democrat Woodrow Wilson win with less than half the popular vote.

questions.q: Which contrast best describes the two main progressive programs in 1912?
options: Roosevelt's New Nationalism accepted regulated big business, while Wilson's New Freedom sought to restore competition
Roosevelt wanted to break up all large firms, while Wilson wanted to regulate them
Both men rejected federal regulation and left business to state governments
Roosevelt wanted free trade and weak regulation, while Wilson wanted a high tariff
questions.explain: Advisers such as Louis Brandeis shaped Wilson's belief that breaking up concentrated power would protect small business.

questions.q: The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 created...
options: A national income tax collected by the Treasury
A central banking system with regional banks
A gold standard that fixed the value of the dollar
A new commission to investigate unfair business practices
questions.explain: The system was meant to supply an elastic currency and reduce panics. A board in Washington oversees 12 regional Reserve Banks.

questions.q: What was the Federal Trade Commission, created in 1914, meant to do?
options: Investigate and stop unfair business practices
Regulate the prices of stocks and bonds on Wall Street
Run the nation's railroads during the war
Set minimum wages for factory workers
questions.explain: Part of Wilson's New Freedom, the FTC was joined by the Clayton Antitrust Act, which gave labor some protection from antitrust suits.

questions.q: The Clayton Antitrust Act of 1914 was welcomed by labor leaders because it...
options: Abolished the American Federation of Labor and similar groups
Guaranteed a federal minimum wage for all workers
Limited use of antitrust law and injunctions against unions
Banned all strikes against railroads and utilities
questions.explain: Samuel Gompers called it labor's "Magna Carta," though courts later interpreted its protections narrowly.

questions.q: Wilson's Underwood Tariff of 1913 was notable because it...
options: Raised tariffs to the highest level in history
Lowered tariffs and included a federal income tax
Ended all tariffs on imported manufactured goods
Created the Federal Reserve as a new national bank
questions.explain: By cutting import duties, it relied on the new income tax to replace lost revenue.

questions.q: After Woodrow Wilson took office in 1913, his administration...
options: Segregated many federal workplaces, including in Washington
Ended segregation in the army and the navy
Hired only Black officials for the top posts in the federal government
Opened the Cabinet to several Black leaders
questions.explain: Black employees in some departments were separated at desks, cafeterias and restrooms, drawing protests from the NAACP and Black newspapers.

questions.q: The NAACP was founded in 1909, in part as a response to...
options: A Supreme Court victory on voting rights for Black citizens in Maryland
The passage of the Dawes Act of 1887
The outcome of the Pullman strike of 1894
Racial violence such as the 1908 Springfield, Illinois, riot
questions.explain: Black leaders, including W.E.B. Du Bois, joined white reformers to fight lynching, disfranchisement and segregation through legal and public campaigns.

questions.q: The Niagara Movement of 1905, led by W.E.B. Du Bois, demanded...
options: Black settlement in Liberia
Full civil rights and an end to racial discrimination
Acceptance of segregation in return for economic aid
Gradual progress through industrial education and patience
questions.explain: Du Bois and others rejected Booker T. Washington's accommodation and called for equal rights and political participation.

questions.q: W.E.B. Du Bois's The Souls of Black Folk (1903) included a famous argument about...
options: The need for vocational training as the way forward
The "color line" as the problem of the century
The benefits that Reconstruction brought to the South
The Great Migration as the answer to Jim Crow
questions.explain: Du Bois combined history, sociology and memoir to attack segregation and criticize Washington's approach.

questions.q: Carter G. Woodson, who founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History in 1915, is remembered for...
options: Founding the Chicago Defender
Running the Tuskegee Institute
Leading the legal team of the NAACP
Promoting Black history, including Negro History Week
questions.explain: Woodson launched Negro History Week in 1926, which grew into Black History Month.

questions.q: The Great Migration refers to the movement of...
options: European immigrants to the farms of the Great Plains
Black Southerners to Northern and Western cities
Farmers to California
Native peoples to Oklahoma
questions.explain: Beginning in the 1910s, millions of Black families left the rural South for jobs and to escape Jim Crow and violence.

questions.q: World War I accelerated the Great Migration mainly by...
options: Banning sharecropping across the South by a federal law
Opening factory jobs as immigration slowed and men enlisted
Closing Southern railroads to Black travelers
Ending Jim Crow laws in several Southern states
questions.explain: Northern industries recruited Black workers, and newspapers like the Chicago Defender encouraged the move.

questions.q: The Chicago Defender, edited by Robert Abbott, encouraged the Great Migration by...
options: Supporting segregation in Northern cities and workplaces
Reporting job openings and criticizing Southern racism
Printing railroad bonds for investors
Opposing the work of the NAACP
questions.explain: The weekly paper circulated widely in the South, often passed from hand to hand, and urged readers to seek better lives in the North.

questions.q: Many Black migrants traveled North by rail, and Pullman porters became important because they...
options: Owned the railroads that ran through the South
Carried news and organized an influential Black labor union
Were exempt from the segregation laws of the South
Managed the daily operation of Union Station in Washington
questions.explain: Porters spread newspapers and news. In 1925 they organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, led by A. Philip Randolph.

questions.q: The Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters was led by...
options: Booker T. Washington
Marcus Garvey
Asa Philip Randolph
Walter White
questions.explain: Randolph won recognition from the Pullman Company in 1937, a landmark victory for Black labor, and later pressed FDR on defense jobs.

questions.q: The Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s was a flowering of...
options: Immigrant labor unions in New York's garment trade district
Black art, literature and music centered in New York
Native American crafts shown in Santa Fe
Southern agriculture and sharecropping
questions.explain: Writers, musicians and artists celebrated Black life and challenged stereotypes, and many were part of the Great Migration generation.

questions.q: Which poet's work, including The Weary Blues (1926), made him a central figure of the Harlem Renaissance?
options: Paul Laurence Dunbar
Countee Cullen
Langston Hughes
Claude McKay
questions.explain: Hughes used jazz and blues rhythms to write about everyday Black life.

questions.q: Zora Neale Hurston's 1937 novel is titled...
options: Native Son
Invisible Man
Their Eyes Were Watching God
The Color Purple
questions.explain: Hurston, trained as an anthropologist, drew on Southern Black folk traditions in her fiction.

questions.q: What did Alain Locke's anthology The New Negro (1925) argue?
options: Black migration to the North should stop
Black Americans were creating a confident new culture
Jazz music should be banned in public
Education was unnecessary for the children of Black families
questions.explain: Locke helped shape the movement by presenting art and writing as expressions of pride and racial equality.

questions.q: Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association appealed to many Black Americans through its emphasis on...
options: Interracial labor organizing
Integration through lawsuits in Northern courts
Racial pride and economic independence
Gradual progress through vocational schools
questions.explain: Garvey's mass movement, with its Black Star Line and "Back to Africa" message, drew thousands of members in the early 1920s.

questions.q: The "Red Summer" of 1919 refers to...
options: A wave of racial violence in many American cities
A wave of strikes by Boston police and coal miners
The arrest of suspected radicals during the Red Scare
A nationwide steel strike led by the AFL
questions.explain: Returning soldiers and migrants competed for jobs and housing, and mobs attacked Black communities in places such as Chicago and Washington, D.C.

questions.q: During the Red Summer of 1919, Black residents of Washington, D.C. responded to white mob attacks by...
options: Calling a citywide general strike
Fighting back to defend themselves and their neighborhoods
Relying entirely on the police for protection
Fleeing the city in large numbers
questions.explain: The riot lasted several days, and its resistance became a sign of a "New Negro" spirit that refused to accept violence passively.

questions.q: The 1921 destruction of the Greenwood district in Tulsa, Oklahoma, involved...
options: A fire that started in a factory and spread through town
A tornado that struck the city and destroyed its homes
A white mob attack on a prosperous Black community
A labor strike in the nearby oil fields
questions.explain: Hundreds of people were killed or wounded, and thousands lost homes and businesses. Survivors and descendants worked for decades to have the event remembered.

questions.q: The Dyer Anti-Lynching Bill, which passed the House in 1922, failed because of...
options: A veto by President Harding
A ruling of the Supreme Court
A national referendum held in every state against the bill
A Senate filibuster by Southern senators
questions.explain: Despite NAACP support, Southern Democrats blocked every federal anti-lynching bill for decades, a tool of the Senate's rules.

questions.q: The Scottsboro case of the 1930s involved...
options: A union boycott of Southern railroads
A fight over school integration in several Alabama towns
Nine Black youths falsely accused of crime in Alabama
A disputed election in Tennessee
questions.explain: The cases reached the Supreme Court, which ruled in Powell v. Alabama that defendants in serious cases need effective counsel, and in Norris v. Alabama that Black jurors could not be excluded.

questions.q: Madam C.J. Walker became a wealthy entrepreneur in the early 1900s by selling...
options: Steel rails and bridges for the railroad companies
Daily and weekly newspapers for Black readers
Hair care and beauty products to Black women
Railroad sleeping cars for long-distance travelers
questions.explain: Walker built a national business, trained sales agents and gave to civic causes. She is often cited as a self-made businesswoman.

questions.q: The Negro Leagues began organizing in 1920 under...
options: Branch Rickey
Satchel Paige
Gus Greenlee
Andrew "Rube" Foster
questions.explain: Excluded from white major leagues, Black players founded their own leagues, which flourished until baseball integrated after 1947.

questions.q: The Immigration Act of 1924 (Johnson-Reed Act) set which kind of limits?
options: A literacy test in the immigrant's own language
National origins quotas that favored Northern and Western Europe
Strict quotas on Mexican and Canadian immigrants
A head tax on every arriving immigrant
questions.explain: Quotas were tied to the 1890 census, which sharply cut arrivals from Southern and Eastern Europe and barred most Asians.

questions.q: Which law of 1921 first imposed numerical limits on European immigration?
options: The Immigration Act of 1917
The Page Act
The Chinese Exclusion Act
The Emergency Quota Act
questions.explain: It capped each nationality at 3 percent of the number of its members living in the US in 1910 and began the era of numerical quotas.

questions.q: Congress passed a literacy test requirement for immigrants in 1917...
options: With Wilson's strong support
After a Supreme Court order
By executive order
Over President Wilson's veto
questions.explain: Nativist sentiment grew during the war years. Wilson had vetoed similar bills before, but Congress now overrode him.

questions.q: Angel Island Immigration Station, opened in 1910, mainly processed...
options: Asian immigrants, especially Chinese, arriving at San Francisco
Irish immigrants arriving by ship in Boston Harbor and New York
Mexican laborers crossing into Texas by train
Italian farmers heading for New York City
questions.explain: Exclusion laws made entry harsh. Detainees often waited weeks or months for hearings, and some carved poems into the walls.

questions.q: The 1907 Gentlemen's Agreement between the US and Japan dealt with...
options: Japan limiting emigration of laborers to the US
A naval treaty limiting the size of battleships in the Pacific
A trade tariff on silk
The annexation of Hawaii
questions.explain: After anti-Japanese hostility in California, Roosevelt arranged for Japan to restrict labor migration rather than pass an exclusion law.

questions.q: Many Mexicans migrated to the United States in the 1910s and 1920s because of...
