options: The Chinese Exclusion Act, which sent laborers east to Texas
The opening of the Panama Canal in 1914
The Mexican Revolution and labor demand in the Southwest
The Dust Bowl, which uprooted Plains farmers
questions.explain: Revolution and violence pushed people north, while farms, mines and railroads recruited workers. The 1924 quotas did not cover the Western Hemisphere.

questions.q: In Buck v. Bell (1927), the Supreme Court upheld...
options: A state compulsory vaccination law
A state literacy test for voters
A state law permitting forced sterilization of people deemed unfit
A state minimum wage law for women
questions.explain: The ruling reflected the influence of the eugenics movement. It has long been criticized as a grave injustice.

questions.q: Margaret Sanger is associated with the early 1900s campaign for...
options: Child labor laws
Prohibition
Settlement houses
Birth control
questions.explain: Sanger opened a clinic in Brooklyn in 1916 and was arrested. She founded organizations that became part of Planned Parenthood.

questions.q: What did the Open Door Notes of 1899, issued by Secretary of State John Hay, seek to do?
options: Annex China
End the Boxer Rebellion by war and occupy Peking
Make Japan a colony
Keep China open to trade with all powers
questions.explain: Hay wanted equal commercial access in China rather than letting any power carve out exclusive zones. The Boxer uprising of 1900 prompted a follow-up note.

questions.q: The Roosevelt Corollary of 1904 to the Monroe Doctrine claimed that the US could...
options: Act as an international police power in the hemisphere
Ban European tourists from Latin America
Recognize new European colonies in the Americas by treaty
Leave Latin American nations alone
questions.explain: Roosevelt argued that "chronic wrongdoing" by Latin American nations justified US intervention. It was applied in places such as the Dominican Republic.

questions.q: Theodore Roosevelt's approach to foreign policy was summed up by the saying...
options: "Speak softly and carry a big stick"
"Entangling alliances with none"
"Peace without victory"
"The world must be made safe for democracy"
questions.explain: The phrase refers to using diplomacy backed by strong military power, as in naval buildup and interventions in Latin America.

questions.q: To build the Panama Canal, the US supported Panama's 1903 independence from...
options: Spain
Mexico
Venezuela
Colombia
questions.explain: After Colombia rejected a treaty, Panama broke away with US naval support, and the new government granted the Canal Zone to the US.

questions.q: The Panama Canal, which opened in 1914, was made possible partly by...
options: Land purchased from Colombia under the Hay-Herran Treaty
Mosquito control that cut yellow fever and malaria
A sea-level design that needed no locks
A Nicaraguan route that avoided the mountains
questions.explain: Dr. William Gorgas's sanitation campaign protected workers. Thousands of laborers, many from the Caribbean, died during construction.

questions.q: The Great White Fleet, which sailed around the world from 1907 to 1909, was meant to...
options: Show American naval power
Support Cuban independence
Escort troops to the Philippines
Enforce the Open Door in China by blockade
questions.explain: Roosevelt sent sixteen battleships on a world tour. The voyage displayed American strength and supported his diplomacy.

questions.q: President Roosevelt won the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize for...
options: Building the Panama Canal on schedule
Arbitrating the Alaska boundary dispute
Negotiating the Open Door policy in China
Mediating the end of the Russo-Japanese War
questions.explain: The Treaty of Portsmouth, signed in New Hampshire in 1905, ended the conflict between Russia and Japan.

questions.q: What did President Taft's "Dollar Diplomacy" try to do?
options: Use private American investment to expand US influence abroad
Cancel the foreign debts that nations owed to the United States
Withdraw American military forces from Asia and Latin America
Raise tariffs on goods coming from Latin America
questions.explain: Taft encouraged American bankers to invest in Latin America and China, believing economic ties would promote stability.

questions.q: Woodrow Wilson's 1914 occupation of Veracruz, Mexico, was a response to...
options: A Mexican invasion of Texas border towns
The arrest of American sailors at Tampico and revolutionary unrest
A Spanish attack on American ships off Cuba
A dispute over control of the Panama Canal Zone and its tolls
questions.explain: Wilson, who called his policy "moral diplomacy," sent forces to pressure the Huerta government, which strained relations with Mexico.

questions.q: The Punitive Expedition of 1916-1917, led by General John J. Pershing, pursued...
options: Emiliano Zapata and his forces
Nicaraguan rebels led by Augusto Sandino
Pancho Villa after his raid on Columbus, New Mexico
German saboteurs who were hiding along the Texas border
questions.explain: Pershing's forces did not capture Villa. The expedition gave the army experience before World War I.

questions.q: The Platt Amendment of 1901 gave the United States the right to...
options: Annex the island of Cuba outright as a new US state
Intervene in Cuba and keep a naval base there
Rule the Philippines as a colony
Buy Puerto Rico from Spain
questions.explain: It was attached to Cuba's constitution as a condition of ending US occupation, and it led to the naval station at Guantanamo Bay.

questions.q: The Insular Cases of 1901 concerned...
options: Rules for the naturalization of immigrants arriving from Europe
Taxes on railroads operating in the West
Whether the Constitution fully applied in new territories
The reach of the Sherman Antitrust Act
questions.explain: The Court decided that territories such as Puerto Rico and the Philippines were "unincorporated," so Congress could treat them differently from states.

questions.q: The Jones Act of 1917 granted what to people of Puerto Rico?
options: Statehood
Independence
The vote for president
US citizenship
questions.explain: Puerto Ricans became citizens just as the US entered World War I, and many served in the military.

questions.q: The Tydings-McDuffie Act of 1934 promised that the Philippines would...
options: Gain independence after a transition period
Become a state of the union within ten years
Rejoin Spain as a province of the empire
Become a British colony in the Pacific
questions.explain: Congress set a ten-year path, interrupted by Japan's invasion in World War II, and the Philippines became independent in 1946.

questions.q: When World War I began in 1914, President Woodrow Wilson told Americans to be...
options: Prepared to enter the war immediately on the Allied side
Neutral in thought as well as deed
Supportive of Germany
Isolated from trade
questions.explain: Most Americans wanted to stay out. Yet strong trade ties with Britain and France and German submarine warfare made neutrality hard.

questions.q: The sinking of the British liner Lusitania by a German submarine in 1915 caused...
options: Immediate US entry into the war on the Allied side
A treaty of friendship between the US and Germany
American outrage because many American passengers died
An end to German submarine warfare for the rest of the war
questions.explain: Of those lost, 128 were Americans. Wilson sent protests, and Germany limited attacks for a time, but the incident hardened opinion against it.

questions.q: What did the Zimmermann Telegram of 1917 propose?
options: Britain would invade Mexico to protect its oil shipping
Japan and the United States would form a military alliance against Germany
Mexico would join the British side in the war
Germany would help Mexico regain land if the US entered the war
questions.explain: British intelligence decrypted the message and gave it to Washington. Published, it angered Americans and helped bring the US into the war.

questions.q: Which German policy announced in early 1917 directly pushed the United States toward war?
options: Unrestricted submarine warfare
The invasion of Belgium
A trade embargo against the United States
A naval blockade of Mexican ports
questions.explain: Germany decided to sink merchant ships on sight to starve Britain, risking American entry because US ships and citizens were at stake.

questions.q: President Wilson asked Congress for a declaration of war in April 1917 by saying the world must be made...
options: Open to free trade
Secure for the Allies
Free from imperial rivalry
Safe for democracy
questions.explain: Wilson presented the war as a fight for democratic principles, and Congress approved it in days, with 50 House members and 6 senators voting no.

questions.q: Jeannette Rankin of Montana, the first woman elected to Congress, is remembered for voting...
options: For national Prohibition in 1919
Against women's suffrage in 1920
For joining the League of Nations and the World Court
Against the declaration of war in 1917
questions.explain: Rankin served in the House and voted no on entering World War I, and in 1941 she cast the lone vote against war with Japan.

questions.q: On December 8, 1941, only one member of Congress voted against declaring war on Japan. She was...
options: Jeannette Rankin
Margaret Chase Smith
Frances Perkins
Clare Boothe Luce
questions.explain: Rankin, a pacifist, voted against the declaration in the House, which otherwise passed overwhelmingly after the Pearl Harbor attack.

questions.q: In 1917 the Senate adopted its first cloture rule, which allows...
options: The president to end filibusters
The House to rule on speeches
A supermajority to limit debate
A simple majority to stop debate
questions.explain: The rule followed a filibuster by a few senators against arming merchant ships. Wilson criticized the "little group of willful men."

questions.q: In 1910 a revolt in the House against Speaker Joseph Cannon resulted in...
options: Cannon's removal from the House
Direct election of the Speaker by voters
The Speaker losing control of the Rules Committee
A ban on committee chairs
questions.explain: Progressive Republicans joined Democrats to curb "Uncle Joe" Cannon's power, shifting authority toward committees and seniority.

questions.q: The Selective Service Act of 1917 provided for...
options: Voluntary enlistment only, with no draft at all
A navy-only force to protect the Atlantic
A draft to raise a national army
Mandatory farm labor for able-bodied men
questions.explain: About 24 million men registered, and millions served, with the new National Army fighting in France under General Pershing.

questions.q: General John J. Pershing led the American Expeditionary Forces and insisted that American troops...
options: Defend Britain from a German invasion across the English Channel
Fight as a distinct American army, not scattered among Allied units
Serve directly under French command in every battle
Remain in training camps in the United States
questions.explain: Pershing resisted merging American troops into Allied armies, and US forces fought in battles such as Meuse-Argonne in late 1918.

questions.q: The 369th Infantry, known as the Harlem Hellfighters, was notable because...
options: It was a Native American infantry unit from the Southwest and Plains
It was a Black regiment that fought with the French and won honors
It guarded the White House and the Capitol in Washington
It was the crew of a Navy ship in the Atlantic
questions.explain: Segregated American forces often put Black soldiers in labor roles. The 369th served with the French army, and many members won the Croix de Guerre.

questions.q: What was the Committee on Public Information, led by George Creel, created to do?
options: Build support for the war through propaganda
Collect taxes to pay for the cost of the war effort
Manage the military draft
Operate the nation's railroads
questions.explain: Posters, films, and speakers by the committee promoted the war and encouraged hostility toward Germans and dissenters.

questions.q: During World War I, Herbert Hoover led the Food Administration, which urged Americans to...
options: Ration food through a strict system of federal law and fines
Stop farming so that farmers could join the army
Eat only imported foods from Britain and France
Save food voluntarily with meatless and wheatless days
questions.explain: Hoover relied on voluntary conservation and slogans, and "to Hooverize" became a word for saving food.

questions.q: What did the War Industries Board, led by Bernard Baruch, try to do?
options: Seize all factories for the federal government for the war
Draft workers into the war industries
Coordinate production and set priorities for war industry
Cut taxes on war industries
questions.explain: The government worked with business to steer resources to war needs, an early experiment in federal economic planning that later inspired New Deal ideas.

questions.q: The United States paid for much of World War I through...
options: Tariff revenue alone
Liberty Loan bond drives and higher taxes
Loans from British and French banks
Sales of public lands in the West
questions.explain: Posters, parades and celebrities urged Americans to buy bonds, while the new income tax rates rose sharply.

questions.q: In 1917 the federal government took control of the nation's railroads through...
options: The Federal Reserve Board
The United States Railroad Administration
The Interstate Commerce Commission acting by itself in 1917
A private railroad trust
questions.explain: Wartime congestion and delays led Wilson to operate the lines under federal management until 1920, an example of increased government power in the war.

questions.q: The Espionage Act of 1917 and Sedition Act of 1918 were used to...
options: Protect immigrants from deportation and unfair trials
Expand free speech for critics during wartime
Prosecute people who criticized the war or the draft
Punish only German diplomats and spies
questions.explain: Many Socialists and pacifists were jailed. Wartime fear and patriotism led to limits on speech that critics later called excessive.

questions.q: In Schenck v. United States (1919), the Supreme Court upheld a conviction for distributing anti-draft leaflets, using which test?
options: "Bad tendency"
"Rule of reason"
"Clear and present danger"
"Strict scrutiny"
questions.explain: Justice Holmes wrote that speech can be restricted when it poses a clear and present danger, a standard later refined in other cases.

questions.q: Socialist leader Eugene V. Debs was imprisoned after a 1918 speech opposing the war, and in 1920 he...
options: Was elected governor of his home state
Ran for president from prison
Left the Socialist Party for the Republicans
Became a federal judge in Indiana
questions.explain: Debs received nearly a million votes in 1920. President Harding commuted his sentence in 1921.

questions.q: Wilson's Fourteen Points, announced in January 1918, called for...
options: An Anglo-American military alliance
Self-determination, free trade, open diplomacy and a League
Harsh reparations and the dismantling of Germany
Cancellation of all Allied war debts
questions.explain: Wilson called for open covenants, freedom of the seas, lower trade barriers and autonomy for subject peoples. The last point proposed an association of nations to keep peace.

questions.q: The war ended with an armistice on...
options: November 11, 1918
April 6, 1917
questions.explain: Fighting stopped at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month, and the date later became a day to honor veterans.

questions.q: The Senate refused to approve the Treaty of Versailles largely because of...
options: A Senate preference for a much stronger League
A Supreme Court ruling against the treaty
The House of Representatives voting the treaty down
Disagreement over the League's Article X and Wilson's refusal to accept reservations
questions.explain: Senators like Lodge wanted reservations protecting Congress's war powers. Wilson refused to compromise, and the treaty failed.

questions.q: Senators who opposed the League of Nations under any circumstances were nicknamed...
options: Mugwumps
Irreconcilables
Stalwarts
Copperheads
questions.explain: Led by figures like William Borah and Hiram Johnson, they feared that membership would draw the US into foreign wars.

questions.q: Woodrow Wilson collapsed in September 1919 during a nationwide speaking tour to win support for what?
options: The Treaty of Versailles and the League of Nations
The Eighteenth Amendment
A new tariff on German goods
Repeal of the Selective Service Act
questions.explain: Wilson collapsed on the tour and suffered a severe stroke on October 2, 1919. He was weakened for the rest of his term, and his wife Edith guarded access to him.

questions.q: Which provision of the Treaty of Versailles placed responsibility for the war on Germany and became the basis for reparations?
options: The clause demilitarizing the Rhineland
The Shandong provision awarding German rights in China to Japan
Article 10, pledging members to protect each other's borders
Article 231, the "war guilt" clause
questions.explain: Germans resented Article 231, which was used to justify reparations. Many historians cite the treaty's resentments as one factor in later instability.

questions.q: The first "Red Scare" of 1919-1920 was fueled by...
options: Strong public support for Soviet Russia after the Revolution of 1917
A close Senate vote on a major labor bill
Fear of communism and anarchism after the Russian Revolution and strikes and bombings
A sharp rise in tariffs on imported goods
questions.explain: Many Americans linked immigrants and labor activism to radicalism, leading to arrests and deportations.

questions.q: The Palmer Raids of 1919-1920, directed by Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer, resulted in...
options: The passage of the Eighteenth Amendment on Prohibition
The arrest and deportation of suspected radicals, many immigrants
New rights for immigrants who entered the United States after the war
The jailing of several members of Congress
questions.explain: Thousands were seized, often without warrants. Public support faded when predictions of revolution proved false.

questions.q: The 1919 Boston police strike made which then-governor a national figure?
options: Calvin Coolidge
Warren Harding
Herbert Hoover
Al Smith
questions.explain: Coolidge declared that there is no right to strike against public safety. His stand helped win him the vice presidential nomination in 1920.

questions.q: The 1919 Seattle general strike and a nationwide steel strike that year...
options: Won union recognition from the major employers in both cities
Ended the wartime wage controls on industry
Led directly to the passage of the Wagner Act
Failed amid fear of radicalism and employer opposition
questions.explain: Postwar inflation sparked strikes, but opponents tied them to Bolshevism, and unions lost ground in the 1920s.

questions.q: Warren Harding's 1920 campaign promised a "return to normalcy," meaning...
options: More progressive reform at home and abroad
Immediate entry into the League of Nations
A calmer postwar era without crusades or foreign entanglements
Higher taxes on business profits and the largest incomes
questions.explain: Voters weary of war and reform elected Harding by a landslide. He died in office in 1923.

questions.q: The Teapot Dome scandal involved...
options: Treasury officials taking bribes from distillers
Veterans' Bureau chief Charles Forbes selling off hospital supplies
Interior Secretary Albert Fall leasing oil reserves for bribes
Army officers selling surplus goods after the war
questions.explain: A Senate investigation led by Thomas Walsh uncovered the bribes, and Fall became the first cabinet member sent to prison.

questions.q: Which president said that the business of the American people was business, and favored low taxes and little regulation?
options: Calvin Coolidge
Woodrow Wilson
Warren Harding
Herbert Hoover
questions.explain: Coolidge's pro-business outlook and Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon's tax cuts typified the Republican governance of the 1920s.

questions.q: The Washington Naval Conference of 1921-1922 produced agreements to...
options: Create a permanent world court at The Hague
Set the reparations that Germany owed to the Allies
Limit the size of major navies
Block Japanese trade across the Pacific
questions.explain: Meeting in the capital, nations agreed on ratios for battleships. The treaties reflected postwar interest in peace without a League.

questions.q: The Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928...
options: Created a League army to stop aggression anywhere in the world
Set up the schedule of German reparation payments
Renounced war as national policy but lacked enforcement
Ended the Great Depression in the United States
questions.explain: Dozens of nations signed, yet there were no penalties for violation, so it became a symbol of the limits of idealism.

questions.q: The Dawes Plan of 1924 helped stabilize Europe by...
options: Reducing German reparation payments and arranging American loans
Cancelling all Allied war debts owed to the United States
Funding the League of Nations from US taxes
Opening German markets to French goods
questions.explain: A cycle developed in which US loans helped Germany pay reparations to Britain and France, who repaid war debts to the US.

questions.q: Henry Ford's Model T became popular in part because...
options: Ford sold it only as a luxury model
Assembly line production made it affordable
Ford paid workers less than competitors to cut costs
The government subsidized car loans for buyers
questions.explain: Ford introduced the moving assembly line in 1913, and prices fell so far that many workers could buy one.

questions.q: Ford's 1914 "five dollar day" was intended partly to...
options: Reduce turnover and let workers afford the cars
Break a union at the Ford plants in Michigan
Fund a political campaign for the Republican party
Hire immigrants only for assembly jobs
questions.explain: Assembly work was monotonous and many workers quit. Higher pay stabilized the workforce and made workers potential customers.

questions.q: How did the spread of automobiles reshape American life in the 1920s?
options: Suburbs, highways, tourism and new industries grew
Cities stopped growing as people moved to farms
Railroads expanded dramatically across the country and replaced roads
Farm size shrank because of new machines
questions.explain: Cars created demand for steel, rubber, oil and roads, and they gave families new mobility.

questions.q: Which new financial practice in the 1920s helped consumers buy cars, radios and appliances?
options: Government grants to pay for new appliances
Federal consumer loans from the Treasury
Buying on installment credit
Company-issued scrip redeemable in goods
questions.explain: Installment plans let people take goods home with small down payments. Debt grew, leaving households vulnerable when the economy turned.

questions.q: KDKA in Pittsburgh, often called the first commercial radio station, began regular broadcasting in 1920 by airing...
options: A major league baseball game from Pittsburgh
A church service from a local congregation
A speech about the war in Europe
Presidential election returns
questions.explain: Radio spread rapidly and created a shared national culture of news, music and advertising.

questions.q: The film The Jazz Singer (1927) was important because it...
options: Was the first full-length animated film
Was the first major feature film with synchronized dialogue and song
Was the first feature film made in color
Was the first film to win a best picture award
questions.explain: Sound films quickly replaced silent films, changing Hollywood and mass entertainment.

questions.q: F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby (1925) is often read as a critique of...
options: The materialism and illusion of the Jazz Age
The hardships of frontier life
The programs of the New Deal
The sacrifices of wartime service in the trenches of France
questions.explain: The novel follows a wealthy man's pursuit of an idealized past, exposing emptiness behind the decade's glitter.

questions.q: The "Lost Generation" writers such as Ernest Hemingway were known for...
options: Praise for the nation's war effort
Strong support for Prohibition
Disillusionment with society after World War I
Westward adventure and pioneer life on the prairie
questions.explain: Many wrote of alienation and living abroad, like Hemingway in Paris, reflecting the war's psychological effects.

questions.q: The "flappers" of the 1920s symbolized...
options: Support for Prohibition and the temperance movement
The old Victorian ideals of modesty and duty
Changing roles and fashions for young women
Support for the work of the WCTU
questions.explain: Short hair, shorter skirts and public smoking and dancing challenged old expectations, although many Americans criticized the trend.

questions.q: The Scopes Trial of 1925 in Dayton, Tennessee, concerned...
options: The enforcement of Prohibition in the rural counties of Tennessee
A state law banning the teaching of evolution in schools
The segregation of public schools in Tennessee
The limits of free speech during wartime
questions.explain: John Scopes was convicted and fined, but the trial, featuring Clarence Darrow and William Jennings Bryan, became a national debate on science and religion.

questions.q: The movement known as Fundamentalism in the 1920s emphasized...
options: The rapid secularization of public life and education
Strong support for the teaching of evolution in public schools
A literal reading of the Bible and resistance to modern science
The Social Gospel of the Progressive reformers
questions.explain: Fundamentalists reacted to modernism in religion and education, and the Scopes Trial brought these tensions into public view.

questions.q: Prohibition, established by the Eighteenth Amendment and enforced by the Volstead Act, led to...
options: A steep drop in all crime
Greater tax revenue from alcohol sales
Illegal speakeasies and the growth of organized crime
Higher church attendance only
questions.explain: Public resistance and bootlegging made enforcement difficult, and gangsters like Al Capone profited.

questions.q: The Twenty-first Amendment of 1933...
options: Repealed Prohibition
Ended the poll tax
Set presidential term limits
Lowered the voting age
questions.explain: Repeal came as the Depression made alcohol taxes and jobs attractive and Prohibition's enforcement problems clear. It is the only amendment that repealed another.

questions.q: The Ku Klux Klan of the 1920s was different from the Reconstruction Klan because it...
options: Appeared only in the Southern states of the old Confederacy
Supported open immigration and equal rights for all
Spread widely in the North and Midwest and targeted Catholics, Jews and immigrants as well as Black people
Was disbanded by an act of Congress in 1920
questions.explain: The second Klan, revived in 1915, claimed millions of members and some political influence before scandals reduced its power. It marched in Washington in 1925.

questions.q: The 1915 film The Birth of a Nation helped revive the Ku Klux Klan by...
options: Glorifying the Reconstruction-era Klan
Condemning the Klan as a danger to the country
Depicting the abolitionists as heroes of the war
Showing the Great Migration of Black families
questions.explain: The film, based on a novel, spread racist myths about Reconstruction, and the NAACP led protests against it.

questions.q: The Sacco and Vanzetti case of the 1920s showed...
options: A major labor union victory in the mills of Massachusetts
A Supreme Court reform of criminal trials
Strong public support for Prohibition
Anti-immigrant and anti-radical fears in a murder trial
questions.explain: The two Italian anarchists were convicted in Massachusetts and executed in 1927, with many believing they were judged for their politics and origins.

questions.q: The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 did what?
options: Declared all Native Americans born in the US citizens
Ended the federal reservation system for all tribes
Returned all of the stolen tribal lands in the West
Created a new system of tribal courts across the whole West
questions.explain: The law came after many Native veterans served in World War I. Some states still blocked Native voting for decades.

questions.q: The 1928 Meriam Report on Native American conditions found that...
options: Allotment and boarding schools had often caused poverty and ill health
The Dawes Act had been a complete and lasting success
Reservations were thriving economically across the whole West
Native education had been excellent in every state
questions.explain: The report criticized federal policy and influenced reforms in the New Deal's Indian Reorganization Act of 1934.

questions.q: What did the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 seek to do?
options: Abolish all reservations by the year 1940 and sell the land
End allotment and encourage tribal self-government
Move tribal members into American cities
Deny tribal land rights in the courts
questions.explain: Under John Collier, the Bureau of Indian Affairs shifted from forced assimilation to supporting tribal governments, though results were mixed.

questions.q: In World War I, Choctaw soldiers used their own language to send messages, an early example of...
options: Trench camouflage
Aerial reconnaissance
Radio broadcasting
Code talking
questions.explain: Their use of Choctaw helped confuse German listeners. The idea was later used on a larger scale by Navajo Marines in World War II.

questions.q: In World War II, the Navajo Code Talkers served in which branch?
options: The Army Air Forces
The Coast Guard
The Merchant Marine
The Marine Corps
questions.explain: They used a code based on the Navajo language that Japanese cryptographers never broke, notably in battles such as Iwo Jima.

questions.q: Why was the Navajo Code Talkers' system so effective in the Pacific?
options: It used the same radio sets as the Japanese navy used
The code used an unwritten language that enemies could not decipher
It relied on traditional Morse code messages
It was published in newspapers around the world
questions.explain: Messages could be sent and decoded in minutes, and the code was kept secret for decades after the war.

questions.q: The Wright brothers' first powered flights took place in 1903 near...
options: Kitty Hawk, North Carolina
Fort Myer, Virginia
Huffman Prairie, Ohio
Dayton, Ohio
questions.explain: Orville and Wilbur Wright flew their Flyer on December 17, 1903. The original aircraft is displayed at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum.

questions.q: Why did the Wright brothers choose Kitty Hawk for their experiments?
options: Steady winds and soft sand dunes suited glider tests
It had large airfields built by the army for test pilots
The army owned the land
It was near their bicycle factory
questions.explain: The location offered reliable winds and a forgiving landing surface, helping them refine control systems.

questions.q: In 1927 Charles Lindbergh became world famous by...
options: Crossing the Pacific by seaplane
Breaking the sound barrier in a jet
Flying around the globe in a balloon without landing
Flying solo nonstop from New York to Paris
questions.explain: His Spirit of St. Louis flight took about 33 hours, and the plane is displayed at the National Air and Space Museum.

questions.q: Amelia Earhart's 1932 achievement was...
options: Flying solo across the Atlantic, the first woman to do so
Founding the nation's first airline
Flying around the world in eight days
Flying solo across the Pacific from Hawaii to California
questions.explain: She became a symbol of women's expanding opportunities before disappearing in 1937 during a round-the-world attempt.

questions.q: What did the Air Commerce Act of 1926 aim to do?
options: Create the United States Air Force as a separate service
Fund the Wright Company with federal grants
Support and regulate civil aviation
Ban private planes from the nation's skies
questions.explain: Congress began federal oversight of airways and pilots, helping the growth of commercial aviation in the late 1920s.

questions.q: The Douglas DC-3, introduced in the mid-1930s, was significant because...
options: It broke the sound barrier in the year it was built
It made air travel profitable and later served as a wartime transport
It was the first jet airliner to cross the Atlantic
It was the first rocket plane to carry the mail
questions.explain: The sturdy plane carried passengers and cargo reliably, and thousands were used by the military in World War II.

questions.q: Brigadier General Billy Mitchell argued in the 1920s that...
options: Cavalry would remain the decisive arm of the army
Submarines were nearly useless in modern naval war
Airpower could sink battleships and transform war
Tanks were obsolete on the modern battlefield
questions.explain: Mitchell's bomber demonstrations were controversial, and he was court-martialed in 1925. His views were later seen as prophetic.

questions.q: The Army Air Forces in World War II expanded from the earlier...
options: Marine Aviation Service
Army Air Corps
Navy Fleet Air
Civil Air Patrol
questions.explain: The service grew enormously during the war and became a separate Air Force in 1947.

questions.q: The stock market crash that began in October 1929 is often traced to...
options: Wartime inflation in the early 1920s that wrecked savings
Heavy speculation and buying stocks on margin
Sudden discoveries of gold
A large federal budget deficit
questions.explain: When prices fell, investors who had borrowed to buy shares were forced to sell, which deepened the collapse.

questions.q: What is the day of the worst panic selling in the 1929 crash, October 29, known as?
options: Black Sunday
Black Tuesday
Red Monday
Bloody Friday
questions.explain: Millions of shares were dumped, and the crash marked the start of a decade-long economic crisis, although it was not its only cause.

questions.q: Which weakness in the 1920s economy contributed to the Great Depression?
options: Wages rose faster than prices
A national shortage of consumer goods in the stores
Excess federal spending
Wealth was concentrated and farm incomes were low
questions.explain: Many families could not buy the goods factories produced, while farmers suffered from low prices, so the boom rested on shaky foundations.

questions.q: The Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930...
options: Cut US tariffs to the lowest level in history and helped trade
Created the first federal income tax
Raised US duties sharply, and other nations answered with barriers
Ended the gold standard in the United States
questions.explain: Most economists believe it worsened the global slump by shrinking trade rather than ending the depression.

questions.q: By 1933 about what share of American workers were unemployed?
options: About one in four
About one in twenty
About one in ten
About one in fifty
questions.explain: Roughly a quarter of the workforce had no job, and many more faced reduced hours and pay.

questions.q: "Hoovervilles" were...
options: New housing projects built by the federal government for veterans
Company towns owned by factories
Army camps for veterans
Shantytowns of homeless and jobless Americans
questions.explain: People built shacks from scrap near cities, and the name reflected blame placed on President Hoover for the hard times.

questions.q: President Herbert Hoover's response to the Depression emphasized...
options: Immediate federal relief jobs for the unemployed on public projects
Nationalization of the banks
Voluntary cooperation and limited federal action at first
Abolition of all tariffs
questions.explain: Hoover believed in individual and local responsibility, though he later created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation to lend to banks and businesses.

questions.q: The Reconstruction Finance Corporation, created in 1932, made loans to...
options: Individual families in need of food and shelter
Foreign governments in debt
State militias and police
Banks, railroads and other businesses
questions.explain: The program tried to prop up the economy from the top, and critics said it did too little for ordinary people.

questions.q: The Bonus Army of 1932 consisted of...
options: Farmers from the Plains who came to demand relief loans
World War I veterans who came to Washington to demand early bonuses
Union coal miners who came to demand a federal minimum wage rate
German immigrants who came to protest the Depression
questions.explain: Thousands camped in the capital, some at Anacostia Flats. After Congress refused, the army cleared the camps, a blow to Hoover's reputation.

questions.q: In the 1932 election, Franklin D. Roosevelt promised the American people...
options: A return to normalcy
A Square Deal
A Fair Deal
A "New Deal"
questions.explain: FDR defeated Hoover in a landslide, running on bold action and activism rather than detailed policies.

questions.q: Franklin Roosevelt's first inaugural address in 1933 included the famous line that...
options: We shall never surrender, we shall fight on the beaches
Ask not what your country can do for you
The only thing we have to fear is fear itself
Government is not the solution to our problem
questions.explain: Roosevelt sought to restore confidence in the midst of a banking crisis and promised swift action.

questions.q: What was FDR's "bank holiday" of March 1933 meant to do?
options: Cancel all personal and business debts across the country
Take over every bank in the nation
Close banks temporarily and restore confidence
Print a brand-new national currency
questions.explain: After the Emergency Banking Act, sound banks reopened, and his radio talk helped persuade people to return deposits.

questions.q: What were FDR's radio addresses to the American public known as?
options: Town halls
Campaign rallies
Fireside chats
War bulletins
questions.explain: Using a relaxed tone, Roosevelt explained policies directly to listeners. His first chat in March 1933 explained the banking crisis.

questions.q: The Glass-Steagall Banking Act of 1933 created the...
options: Federal Reserve
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
Securities and Exchange Commission
Social Security Board
questions.explain: By insuring deposits it ended the cycle of bank runs, and it also separated commercial banking from investment banking.

questions.q: The Pecora hearings of 1933-1934 in the Senate investigated...
options: The growth of labor unions
Safety conditions on railroads and in mines
Corruption in the Bureau of Indian Affairs
Wall Street practices before the crash
questions.explain: Revelations about stock manipulation and risky banking built support for the Securities Exchange Act and the SEC.

questions.q: What was the Securities and Exchange Commission, created in 1934, meant to do?
options: Run the nation's largest banks directly
Collect the federal income tax from workers every month
Fix the wages of industrial workers by law
Regulate the stock market and require honest disclosure
questions.explain: The agency aimed to restore investor confidence and prevent fraud, and Joseph P. Kennedy was its first chairman.

questions.q: The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) put young men to work on...
options: Building ships and docks for the navy
Manufacturing arms and ammunition for the army and navy
Teaching in rural schools in poor regions
Planting trees, building parks and other conservation work
questions.explain: Millions of men lived in camps, earning pay that they largely sent home, and the program improved forests and parks.

questions.q: What was the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) created to do?
options: Regulate the nation's largest commercial banks and trusts
Set shipping rates for the Southern railroads
Pay farmers not to plant crops on their land
Control floods and provide cheap power in a poor region
questions.explain: The TVA built dams and brought power to rural areas, but also sparked debate about government competition with private utilities.

questions.q: The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 tried to raise crop prices by...
options: Opening new farm land on the Western frontier
Ending federal farm subsidies and price supports
Paying farmers to reduce production
Banning tractors from farms on the Plains
questions.explain: Reducing supply was intended to lift prices, but tenant farmers and sharecroppers often lost land because owners took payments and cut workers.

questions.q: The National Industrial Recovery Act of 1933 created codes of fair competition under...
options: The Social Security Board and its old-age pension plan
The National Recovery Administration and its Blue Eagle
The Works Progress Administration and its jobs
The Federal Reserve and its regional banks
questions.explain: Businesses cooperated on prices and wages, but critics complained of favoring big firms. The Supreme Court struck it down in 1935.

questions.q: What did the Supreme Court find in Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States (1935)?
options: Social Security was unconstitutional on its face and in its taxes
The NRA gave the executive too much lawmaking power and regulated local business
The AAA was a valid use of the taxing power
The TVA could not sell electric power to cities
questions.explain: The unanimous ruling struck down a central part of the First New Deal and worried FDR about further decisions.

questions.q: In United States v. Butler (1936) the Supreme Court struck down...
options: The Agricultural Adjustment Act's processing tax
The Social Security Act's payroll tax on workers and employers
The Wagner Act's labor protections
The TVA's power projects
questions.explain: The Court said the farm program regulated agriculture beyond Congress's powers. Congress later passed a revised farm law.

questions.q: The Works Progress Administration (WPA), created in 1935, provided...
options: Cash grants paid directly to farmers who agreed to cut crops
Government jobs on projects such as roads, buildings and arts
Insurance for bank deposits up to a set limit
Federal recognition of labor unions in factories
questions.explain: Led by Harry Hopkins, the WPA employed millions of people, including artists and writers, and left behind many schools, bridges and parks.

questions.q: Which WPA program interviewed formerly enslaved people, producing narratives now in the Library of Congress?
options: The Civilian Conservation Corps
The Rural Electrification Administration
The Public Works Administration
The Federal Writers' Project
questions.explain: Writers collected thousands of accounts in the 1930s, an invaluable record of the experience of slavery.

questions.q: The Farm Security Administration photographers, including Dorothea Lange and Walker Evans, documented...
options: The coming of the war in Europe
Industrial prosperity in the great cities of the North
Rural poverty and the effects of the Depression
The lives of Hollywood movie stars
questions.explain: Their images helped build public support for relief. The collection is held by the Library of Congress.

questions.q: Dorothea Lange's 1936 photograph Migrant Mother became an icon of...
options: Wartime industry and the rise of defense plants
The Dust Bowl dams and the new reservoirs
Hollywood fame and the stars of the movies
Families uprooted by the Depression
questions.explain: The portrait of a pea picker in California put a human face on the crisis and is among the best-known images in the Library of Congress.

questions.q: Folklorist Alan Lomax recorded Woody Guthrie for which institution in 1940?
options: The Smithsonian Institution's folk art museum
The Federal Reserve's archive of recordings
The Library of Congress's folk song archive
The National Archives' sound collection
questions.explain: Lomax and his father preserved American folk music in the 1930s and 1940s, helping to document regional music traditions.

questions.q: The Public Works Administration (PWA), led by Harold Ickes, concentrated on...
options: Short-term jobs for artists, writers, actors and musicians
Subsidies for farmers who cut production
Large projects such as dams, bridges and public buildings
Regulation of the nation's banks and exchanges
questions.explain: Its projects were often big and carefully planned, while the WPA put more people to work quickly.

questions.q: The Social Security Act of 1935 created...
options: Free hospital care for every citizen of the United States
Old-age pensions and unemployment insurance
A national minimum wage
A guaranteed right to strike
questions.explain: Funded by payroll taxes, the program was a cornerstone of the new welfare state, though it excluded many farm and domestic workers.

questions.q: Many Black workers were initially left out of Social Security because...
options: It applied only to workers who lived in the Northern states
The act excluded agricultural and domestic workers
It counted only veterans of the war
It required a college degree to qualify
questions.explain: The exclusions covered farm and household workers, a majority of Black workers in 1935; historians debate whether Southern pressure or tax-collection concerns drove them.

questions.q: Frances Perkins, who helped create Social Security, was the first woman to...
options: Serve in a US Cabinet
Serve as a senator
Sit on the Supreme Court
Be vice president
questions.explain: Roosevelt named Perkins Secretary of Labor in 1933, and she remained in the post throughout his presidency.

questions.q: The Wagner Act of 1935 protected workers' right to...
options: Organize unions and bargain collectively
Retire with a government pension at the age of 65
Receive a federal minimum wage
Strike without any legal limits
questions.explain: It created the National Labor Relations Board to guard against unfair practices, and union membership grew rapidly.

questions.q: The Congress of Industrial Organizations (CIO), led by John L. Lewis, differed from the AFL by...
options: Organizing all workers in an industry, skilled or not
Organizing only craft workers in skilled trades and crafts
Excluding industrial workers from membership
Endorsing only Republican candidates
questions.explain: The CIO organized mass-production workers in steel and autos, and rivalry with the AFL pushed both to grow.

questions.q: The 1936-1937 Flint sit-down strike ended with...
options: A court order to stop the strike and clear the plants
A federal takeover of the General Motors plants
The union dissolving after a defeat
General Motors recognizing the United Auto Workers
questions.explain: Workers occupied the plants, and Michigan's governor refused to send troops, leading to a landmark union victory.

questions.q: The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 established...
options: A federal minimum wage, maximum hours and child labor limits
Old-age pensions funded by payroll taxes
The right to bargain collectively with employers
Insurance for unemployed workers across the whole nation
questions.explain: It set initial minimums of 25 cents an hour and aimed at ending child labor in industry, a goal that earlier courts had blocked.

questions.q: After the Supreme Court struck down parts of the New Deal, FDR proposed in 1937 to...
options: Add new justices for each justice over age 70
Remove the Court's power to review laws
Impeach several of the justices
Amend the Constitution to limit the Court to seven justices
questions.explain: He argued the plan would help overworked courts, but critics saw an attempt to control the Court, and Congress rejected it.

questions.q: FDR's Court-packing plan failed in the Senate partly because...
options: The Supreme Court ruled the plan unconstitutional
Voters rejected it in a national referendum
Many in his own party saw a threat to judicial independence
The House passed a bill forbidding any change in the Court's size
questions.explain: Even Democrats, including leaders of the Judiciary Committee, opposed it, and the Court's shift in 1937 reduced urgency.

questions.q: What was an effect of the Court-packing fight on the New Deal?
options: It led Congress to raise the Court to fifteen justices
It led the Court to strike down Social Security
It ended the New Deal at once
It weakened FDR's standing in Congress even as the Court began upholding New Deal laws
questions.explain: The plan strengthened conservative opposition in Congress, though the Court soon upheld laws such as the Wagner Act and Social Security.

questions.q: Critics of the New Deal from the left, such as Huey Long, proposed...
options: "Share Our Wealth" to redistribute fortunes
A monthly pension funded by a transactions tax
Abolition of Social Security and the WPA
A federal bank to refinance farm mortgages
questions.explain: Long's plan promised every family a guaranteed income, and it pressed Roosevelt to move further left in 1935.

questions.q: Father Charles Coughlin, a radio priest, initially supported FDR but later...
options: Became a harsh critic of the New Deal
Became FDR's running mate in 1936
Became the head of the CIO
Joined the cabinet as Secretary of Labor
questions.explain: His broadcasts reached millions, and by the late 1930s his rhetoric turned angry and openly antisemitic.

questions.q: The Townsend Plan proposed...
options: A new national highway system across the whole country
A federal bank to make loans to small farmers
Monthly payments to older Americans funded by a transactions tax
A plan for land reform in the Southern states
questions.explain: Dr. Francis Townsend's idea gained millions of followers and helped build pressure for Social Security.

questions.q: In 1936 Franklin Roosevelt won reelection by...
options: Winning the electoral vote while losing the popular vote
A landslide, carrying every state except Maine and Vermont
A narrow electoral college majority
A runoff vote in the House of Representatives
questions.explain: The New Deal coalition of Southerners, workers, farmers, Black voters, and urban voters gave him a huge victory over Alf Landon.

questions.q: The "New Deal coalition" that supported Roosevelt's Democrats included...
options: Only owners of large businesses and banks
Urban workers, Southerners, farmers, Black voters and ethnic groups
Only voters in the rural districts
Only voters in the Midwest and the Mountain West states
questions.explain: This broad alliance made the Democratic Party the majority party for decades.

questions.q: By the mid-1930s many Black voters shifted from the Republican to the Democratic Party because...
options: Democrats had ended segregation in the South by law
New Deal relief programs offered help in the Depression
Republicans had passed Jim Crow laws
Black leaders opposed the WPA
questions.explain: Despite discrimination in some programs, Black Americans benefited from relief, and Eleanor Roosevelt's visible support helped.

questions.q: Mary McLeod Bethune's role in the Roosevelt administration was as...
options: Director of Negro Affairs in the National Youth Administration and head of an informal "Black Cabinet"
Secretary of Labor in FDR's Cabinet
US Ambassador to the League of Nations in Geneva
Law clerk to a Supreme Court justice
questions.explain: Bethune advised the president on Black concerns and founded a college that became Bethune-Cookman University.

questions.q: Eleanor Roosevelt was unusual among first ladies because she...
options: Held press conferences, traveled and advocated for causes
Stayed out of public life entirely during the Depression years
Served as a member of Congress from New York
Commanded a women's army corps in Europe
questions.explain: She served as the president's "eyes and ears," campaigned for civil rights and relief, and wrote a newspaper column.

questions.q: In 1939, Marian Anderson sang at the Lincoln Memorial after...
options: Her European tour had ended early because of war
Her concert at the Capitol was cancelled by the Senate Sergeant at Arms
The Daughters of the American Revolution refused her Constitution Hall
Howard University had banned public concerts
questions.explain: Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from the DAR in protest, and Interior Secretary Harold Ickes arranged the Easter Sunday concert before a huge crowd.

questions.q: Marian Anderson's Easter Sunday concert in 1939 at the Lincoln Memorial drew an audience of about...
options: 750 people
7,500 people
75,000 people
750,000 people
questions.explain: The open-air event, broadcast by radio, became a landmark of the civil rights story and tied the memorial to equal rights.

questions.q: At the 1922 dedication of the Lincoln Memorial, the seating arrangement was notable because...
options: The ceremony was fully integrated
Only veterans of the war were allowed to attend the ceremony
Black guests were placed in a segregated section
Only members of Congress were seated
questions.explain: Robert Moton of Tuskegee Institute, the only Black speaker, had to tone down his address, and Black guests were roped off in a separate section, a contrast with Marian Anderson's 1939 concert.

questions.q: The Jefferson Memorial, dedicated in 1943, was designed by John Russell Pope in the style of which ancient building?
options: The Colosseum in Rome
The Pantheon in Rome
Hagia Sophia in Constantinople
The Parthenon in Athens
questions.explain: Pope modeled the domed memorial on the Pantheon, and it opened in the 200th anniversary year of Jefferson's birth.

questions.q: The Jefferson Memorial's inscriptions include words from...
options: The Gettysburg Address, delivered by Lincoln in 1863
The Fourteen Points of 1918
The Atlantic Charter of 1941
The Declaration of Independence
questions.explain: The memorial displays passages from Jefferson's writings on liberty and religious freedom.

questions.q: The Dust Bowl of the 1930s was caused by drought combined with...
options: The eruption of a volcano in the Rocky Mountains
Plowing up grasslands and poor farming practices
Unusually heavy snowfall on the Plains
A flood of the Mississippi River
questions.explain: When the topsoil dried, winds lifted it into huge dust storms, especially on the southern Plains.

questions.q: "Black Sunday," April 14, 1935, is remembered as...
options: The day the stock market crashed
One of the worst dust storms of the Dust Bowl
A major hurricane that struck the Gulf Coast in April
A riot in Washington, D.C.
questions.explain: A huge black cloud swept across the Plains, and the event helped win support for soil conservation.

questions.q: John Steinbeck's novel The Grapes of Wrath (1939) tells the story of...
options: Factory workers in Pittsburgh during the strikes
Dust Bowl migrants traveling to California
Soldiers fighting in Europe
Immigrants at Ellis Island
questions.explain: The Joad family's journey brought national attention to the plight of "Okies" and migrant labor.

questions.q: The Soil Conservation Service, created in 1935, promoted...
options: Mining coal and iron ore on public land
Building canals and locks across the Plains
Contour plowing, terracing and cover crops
Cutting forests to clear land for farms
questions.explain: Led by Hugh Bennett, it worked to hold soil in place and also supported programs such as planting windbreaks.

questions.q: What did the Rural Electrification Administration (1935) aim to do?
options: Bring electric power to farm homes
Build highways across farm country
Provide food stamps to rural families
Train rural young people as soldiers
questions.explain: Private utilities had skipped rural areas as unprofitable, so the federal government supported cooperatives to bring lines to farms.

questions.q: Hoover Dam, finished in 1936 on the Colorado River, was built to...
options: Open the Colorado River to ocean-going ships
Irrigate the farmland of the Great Plains
Control floods and supply water and power to the Southwest
Provide electric power to the Tennessee Valley
questions.explain: The project employed thousands during the Depression and supported growth in cities like Los Angeles and Las Vegas.

questions.q: The Gold Reserve Act of 1934 did what?
options: Brought back the gold standard of the 1890s
Banned all private banks
Ended private ownership of gold coins and raised gold's price
Created the first national currency in the history of the US
questions.explain: It reflected the move away from gold as the base of the money supply, which gave the government more flexibility.

questions.q: What was the main effect of the 1937-1938 recession?
options: It showed that cutting federal spending too soon could hurt recovery
It ended the Depression for good in 1938
It led to a sharp increase in tariffs
It brought an end to Social Security payments for retirees
questions.explain: Roosevelt reduced spending and the economy slid back, leading him to resume spending in 1938.

questions.q: Which economist argued that government spending could help end depressions, influencing FDR's later policies?
options: Adam Smith
Milton Friedman
John Maynard Keynes
Karl Marx
questions.explain: Keynes's ideas encouraged deficit spending to boost demand. The huge spending of World War II seemed to confirm his view.

questions.q: What was the Twentieth Amendment (1933), which moved presidential inauguration to January 20, meant to do?
options: Limit presidents to two terms
Give the District of Columbia a vote in presidential elections
Lower the voting age to 18
Shorten the gap between election and taking office
questions.explain: The old March date left a long period between election and inauguration, which proved harmful during the winter of 1932-1933.

questions.q: FDR is the only president to...
options: Serve as a general
Be elected without a party
Be a Supreme Court justice
Be elected four times
questions.explain: He won in 1932, 1936, 1940 and 1944, and the Twenty-second Amendment later limited presidents to two terms.

questions.q: Franklin Roosevelt's polio affected how he...
options: Used a wheelchair and braces and limited photographs of them
Served as an officer in the army during World War I in France
Wrote bills for Congress by himself
Avoided speaking on the radio and in public
questions.explain: The disease paralyzed his legs in 1921. He rebuilt his career and founded a therapy center at Warm Springs, Georgia.

questions.q: The FDR Memorial in Washington is notable for being arranged as...
options: A single large dome over a statue
A tall obelisk beside a pool
A walled courtyard around a garden with a single fountain
Four outdoor "rooms," one for each of his terms
questions.explain: The memorial, dedicated in 1997, uses water, stone and quotations to tell the story of the Depression and the war years.

questions.q: The FDR Memorial includes a statue of Eleanor Roosevelt, who after her husband's death worked with which new international organization?
options: The League of Nations
The World Bank
NATO
The United Nations
questions.explain: She served as a US delegate to the UN and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

questions.q: The FDR Memorial includes a statue of which pet, a famous companion of the president?
options: Fala, his Scottish terrier
Checkers
Buddy
Millie
questions.explain: Fala traveled with Roosevelt and became a celebrity, and the statue is placed beside the seated figure of the president.

questions.q: The Four Freedoms outlined by FDR in January 1941 were freedom of speech and worship, and freedom from...
options: Taxes and debt
Disease and ignorance
Prejudice and injustice
Want and fear
questions.explain: Roosevelt described these as basic rights everywhere in the world, goals that guided his case for aiding the Allies.

questions.q: Norman Rockwell's 1943 paintings of the Four Freedoms were used to...
options: Recruit navy pilots
Sell war bonds
Promote Prohibition
Raise relief funds
questions.explain: The Saturday Evening Post published the series, and a traveling exhibition sold over $130 million in war bonds.

questions.q: In his 1937 Quarantine Speech, FDR suggested that...
options: The US should join the League of Nations
Americans should stay silent about all foreign wars
Japan should be rewarded for its restraint
Aggressor nations should be isolated like a disease
questions.explain: The speech met a negative reaction from isolationists, so Roosevelt did not follow it with immediate action.

questions.q: What were the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s intended to do?
options: Help Britain and France with weapons, supplies and loans
Create a national peacetime draft
Rebuild the navy for service in the Pacific
Keep the US out of foreign wars by limiting arms and loans
questions.explain: Passed after the disillusion of World War I, they banned loans and arms to belligerents, which limited Roosevelt's options.

questions.q: The Nye Committee of 1934-1936 in the Senate investigated...
options: Corruption in the Teapot Dome oil leases
The relief policy of the Hoover administration in 1932
The causes of the Dust Bowl on the Plains
The role of arms makers and bankers in drawing the US into World War I
questions.explain: Its findings fed the belief that "merchants of death" had dragged the nation into war, strengthening isolationism.

questions.q: The 1939 "cash and carry" revision of the Neutrality Act allowed...
options: Warring nations to buy arms if they paid and carried them away
A peacetime draft for American men
Naval convoys to protect British merchant ships at sea
Arms loans to China and Britain
questions.explain: Because Britain and France controlled the seas, this change actually favored the Allies.

questions.q: The "Destroyers for Bases" deal of 1940 involved...
options: Selling American warships to Germany for cash
Building new naval bases in Panama and Cuba
Trading 50 old US destroyers for leases on British bases
Ending the peacetime draft in the United States that year
questions.explain: The arrangement helped Britain and expanded US defenses without Senate treaty approval, a step toward involvement.

questions.q: The Lend-Lease Act of March 1941 allowed the president to...
options: Send American troops to fight alongside the British in Europe
Declare war on Germany and Italy
Supply war materials to nations vital to US defense
Draft women into the army and navy
questions.explain: Roosevelt compared it to lending a neighbor a garden hose to put out a fire. It made the US the "arsenal of democracy."

questions.q: FDR called the United States the "arsenal of democracy" in a 1940 fireside chat to...
options: Announce a declaration of war on Germany
Justify strict neutrality in the European war for good
Argue for making weapons for nations fighting the Axis
Announce a nationwide program of rationing
questions.explain: He urged massive production while keeping the US formally out of the war.

questions.q: The Atlantic Charter of August 1941 was a joint statement by...
options: Roosevelt and Stalin dividing postwar Europe between them
Wilson and Clemenceau ending the First World War
Roosevelt and Churchill setting war aims like self-determination
Truman and Attlee planning the United Nations
questions.explain: The leaders met off Newfoundland and pledged to oppose territorial aggrandizement and support free trade and freedom of the seas.

questions.q: The Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 was notable as...
options: A ban on all military conscription during peacetime
A draft of women for factory work
The first peacetime draft in US history
The end of the draft in wartime
questions.explain: With war raging in Europe, Congress required men aged 21 to 35 to register, building up the army before Pearl Harbor.

questions.q: The America First Committee of 1940-1941 argued for...
options: Joining the Axis powers
Declaring war on Germany at once and sending troops
Sending more aid to Britain
Staying out of the war in Europe
questions.explain: Its members, including Charles Lindbergh, feared that intervention would harm the US. It dissolved after Pearl Harbor.

questions.q: In 1941 the United States responded to Japan's advance into Southeast Asia by...
options: Freezing Japanese assets and cutting oil exports
Declaring war on Japan at once
Offering Japan a new trade treaty
Withdrawing American forces from the Philippines and Guam
questions.explain: The embargo threatened Japan's war machine, which raised tension as negotiations failed in late 1941.

questions.q: Japan attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor on...
options: June 6, 1944
September 1, 1939
December 7, 1941
April 6, 1917
questions.explain: The surprise strike on Hawaii killed about 2,400 Americans and damaged much of the Pacific Fleet's battleships.

questions.q: FDR called December 7, 1941, "a date which will live in infamy" in a speech to...
options: The Supreme Court
The United Nations
A joint session of Congress
A radio audience only
questions.explain: Congress declared war on Japan within hours of his address, and Germany and Italy declared war on the US days later.

questions.q: Which US ship, sunk at Pearl Harbor with most of its crew, now has a memorial over its wreck?
options: USS Missouri
USS Maine
USS Constitution
USS Arizona
questions.explain: The battleship exploded after a bomb hit, and over a thousand crew members died, more than any other ship that day.

questions.q: American aircraft carriers escaped destruction at Pearl Harbor mainly because...
options: They were away from port at the time
They were protected by new anti-aircraft batteries
They were sheltered inside the harbor's torpedo nets
Japan deliberately spared them
questions.explain: The absence of carriers was crucial, as they became the key weapons in the Pacific naval war that followed.

questions.q: After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, Germany and Italy...
options: Made peace with Britain
Remained neutral in the Pacific war and the Atlantic war
Declared war on the United States
Launched an attack on Mexico
questions.explain: Hitler's declaration on December 11 removed any debate about fighting in Europe, linking the two wars.

questions.q: Which strategy did the Allies adopt in 1941-1942 regarding the two main theaters?
options: Defeat Germany first while holding Japan
Defeat Japan first and then turn to Europe
Fight only in Asia and avoid Europe
Wait for the Soviet Union to win alone
questions.explain: Because Germany was seen as the greater threat, the Allies agreed to make its defeat the priority while holding the line against Japan.

questions.q: The Pentagon, begun in September 1941, was built in roughly how long?
options: About sixteen months
About five years
About ten years
About three months
questions.explain: Ground was broken on September 11, 1941, and the huge War Department headquarters in Arlington, Virginia, was finished in January 1943.

questions.q: The Pentagon's unusual five-sided shape was a result of...
options: An architect's copy of a European star fort
The shape of the first planned site, which was bounded by roads
A plan to give each of five War Department bureaus its own side
A law requiring federal buildings to have five sides
questions.explain: The first planned site near Arlington Farms was an irregular five-sided plot. The site moved, but the design was already advanced and the pentagon shape was kept.

questions.q: The general who oversaw the Pentagon's construction before leading the Manhattan Project was...
options: Leslie Groves
George Marshall
Dwight Eisenhower
Douglas MacArthur
questions.explain: As a deputy chief of construction in the Army Corps of Engineers, Groves oversaw the project and then took charge of the atomic bomb effort.

questions.q: Which general served as US Army Chief of Staff during most of World War II and shaped the creation of a huge army?
options: Omar Bradley
Douglas MacArthur
George Patton
George C. Marshall
questions.explain: Marshall organized the army's expansion and later, as Secretary of State, gave his name to a European recovery plan.

questions.q: The Joint Chiefs of Staff were established in 1942 to...
options: Coordinate strategy among the US armed services
Run the national draft and the registration of men
Lead the Navy's fleets in the Pacific
Make laws for the armed forces
questions.explain: Created to match the British Chiefs of Staff, the group helped plan operations with allies.

questions.q: Which military leader served as Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, leading the D-Day invasion?
options: Douglas MacArthur
Chester Nimitz
Omar Bradley
Dwight D. Eisenhower
questions.explain: Eisenhower coordinated American, British and Canadian forces and later became president.

questions.q: D-Day, the Allied landing in Normandy, took place on...
options: December 7, 1941
June 6, 1944
August 6, 1945
questions.explain: More than 150,000 Allied troops crossed the English Channel, and the beachheads opened a second front against Germany.

questions.q: American forces landed on which two Normandy beaches on D-Day?
options: Utah and Omaha
Gold and Juno
Sword and Gold
Juno and Sword
questions.explain: The British and Canadians took the other three. Omaha Beach saw especially heavy US casualties.

questions.q: Why did the Allies open a "second front" in France in 1944?
options: To relieve pressure on the Soviets and defeat Germany
To prepare an invasion of Japan from China
To protect neutral Spain from a German attack in Iberia
To save Italy from an invasion by Germany
questions.explain: The Soviets had long asked for such a front, and the invasion forced Germany to fight on two fronts.

questions.q: The Battle of Midway in June 1942 was a turning point in the Pacific because...
options: Japan captured Hawaii and the West Coast
The US lost all of its aircraft carriers
The battle ended the war in the Pacific
US forces sank four Japanese carriers
questions.explain: Using intelligence from broken codes, the US destroyed much of Japan's carrier strength, allowing the US to go on the offensive.

questions.q: What did the US strategy of "island hopping" in the Pacific aim to do?
options: Capture every island in the Pacific one after another
Seize selected islands and bypass others on the way to Japan
Avoid islands and attack by sea only
Invade China first and then Japan
questions.explain: Taking key islands gave airfields and cut off the rest, saving time and lives.

questions.q: Which Associated Press photographer took the 1945 photograph of Marines raising the flag on Iwo Jima?
options: Margaret Bourke-White
Robert Capa
Joe Rosenthal
Alfred Eisenstaedt
questions.explain: Rosenthal's picture, taken on Mount Suribachi on February 23, 1945, won a Pulitzer Prize and inspired the Marine Corps War Memorial near Arlington.

questions.q: The Doolittle Raid of April 1942 was important because...
options: It ended the war in the Pacific within a year of the raid
It destroyed most of Japan's fleet
It captured the city of Tokyo
It showed Japan was vulnerable and lifted American morale
questions.explain: Bombers flew from a carrier to strike Japan. The raid caused little damage but boosted American spirits after Pearl Harbor.

questions.q: The Battle of the Bulge, December 1944-January 1945, was...
options: A Japanese attack on Hawaii in late 1944
A German counteroffensive in the Ardennes that failed
An Allied landing in Italy in the summer of 1943 at Salerno
A siege of the city of Moscow
questions.explain: Germany's last major offensive in the West ended in defeat, leaving it short of men and fuel.

questions.q: V-E Day, marking Germany's surrender, came on...
options: August 15, 1945
June 6, 1944
November 11, 1918
questions.explain: Allied leaders celebrated the end of the war in Europe, but fighting in the Pacific continued.

questions.q: At the Yalta Conference in February 1945, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin agreed to...
options: Divide Germany into zones and form a United Nations
End the war in Asia by treaty with Japan
Re-create the League of Nations in Geneva with a new charter
Divide Italy among the Allied powers
questions.explain: The meeting also promised free elections in Eastern Europe and Soviet entry into war against Japan, but the elections issue later caused conflict.

questions.q: Which president attended the Potsdam Conference in July 1945?
options: Franklin Roosevelt
Herbert Hoover
Dwight Eisenhower
Harry S. Truman
questions.explain: Roosevelt had died in April, and Truman met Churchill and Stalin and issued a warning to Japan.

questions.q: Franklin Roosevelt died in April 1945 and was succeeded by...
options: Harry S. Truman
Henry Wallace
Thomas Dewey
Dwight Eisenhower
questions.explain: Truman had served as vice president for only a few months and learned about the atomic bomb only after taking office.

questions.q: The Tehran Conference of 1943 was the first meeting of Roosevelt, Churchill and...
options: Charles de Gaulle
Josip Broz Tito
Chiang Kai-shek
Stalin
questions.explain: The Big Three discussed opening a second front in Europe, a step that Stalin pressed for.

questions.q: The Casablanca Conference of 1943 produced the Allied call for...
options: Unconditional surrender of the Axis powers
A separate peace with Italy
A new League of Nations
Large reparations from Germany, paid in gold and goods
questions.explain: Roosevelt announced the demand, intended to reassure the Soviets and avoid a repeat of the Versailles outcome.

questions.q: The Senate approved the UN Charter in 1945 by a vote of...
options: Unanimously by voice
89 to 2
questions.explain: The lopsided result contrasted with the Senate's rejection of the League of Nations, reflecting changes in opinion after the war.

questions.q: What was the Holocaust?
options: The Japanese capture of Manila in 1942
Nazi Germany's systematic murder of about six million Jews
The firebombing of Dresden in 1945
Stalin's purges of the Soviet Union
questions.explain: The Nazis and collaborators also murdered millions of others, including Roma and people with disabilities, in camps and mass shootings.

questions.q: The 1939 voyage of the SS St. Louis, carrying Jewish refugees, illustrated...
options: A successful rescue of refugees by a neutral nation like Cuba
The difficulty of finding refuge when nations including the US refused entry
The strength of American immigration policy
German humanitarian aid to Jewish refugees
questions.explain: The ship was turned away from Cuba and the US, and many passengers later died in the Holocaust after returning to Europe.

questions.q: The 1939 Wagner-Rogers bill, which failed in Congress, would have...
options: Created a fund for refugee families
Ended the national origins quota system
Admitted 20,000 Jewish refugee children from Germany
Funded the formation of the United Nations in San Francisco
questions.explain: Opposition, rooted in nativism and anti-Jewish prejudice, kept it from passing.

questions.q: What did the War Refugee Board, created by FDR in 1944, attempt to do?
options: Run Japanese internment camps on the West Coast and in Hawaii
Regulate wartime rationing of food and fuel
Supply aid to the Soviets under Lend-Lease
Rescue and aid civilians threatened by the Nazis
questions.explain: The agency helped save many thousands of Jews and other civilians, though many historians note it was created late.

questions.q: US troops liberating Nazi camps in 1945 prompted General Eisenhower to...
options: Hide the facts from the American public until the war ended
Order the camps closed at once
Offer clemency to the camp guards
Invite Congress members and journalists to see the evidence
questions.explain: He wanted the world to see what had happened, to prevent denial. Photographs from the camps shocked Americans.

questions.q: The Nuremberg Trials after World War II, in which US Supreme Court Justice Robert Jackson served as chief prosecutor, tried...
options: Japanese emperors for treason against the state and army
Soviet generals for desertion in battle
American spies for treason in wartime
Nazi leaders for war crimes and crimes against humanity
questions.explain: The trials established that individuals can be held responsible for atrocities even when they followed orders.

questions.q: Which wartime agency directed the conversion of factories to war production?
options: The Works Progress Administration
The Civilian Conservation Corps
The War Production Board
The National Recovery Administration
questions.explain: Created in 1942, it allocated scarce materials and set production priorities, with auto plants turning to military goods.

questions.q: The Office of Price Administration (OPA) organized rationing of items such as...
options: Newspapers and magazines
Books, school supplies and magazines
Gasoline, sugar, meat and tires
Telephone calls and mail
questions.explain: Ration books limited purchases to keep supplies for the military and to hold down prices.

questions.q: Americans grew "victory gardens" during World War II to...
options: Raise money to pay federal taxes
Produce food at home and save supplies for the troops
Compete for prizes at county and state fairs
Replace the farms of the Midwest as a source of food for the army
questions.explain: Millions of families planted vegetables in yards and parks, easing demands on commercial food supplies.

questions.q: War bonds during World War II helped by...
options: Replacing the federal income tax entirely for the war years
Raising money and absorbing cash to limit inflation
Funding the GI Bill after the war
Paying for the rationing program
questions.explain: Posters, rallies and celebrities urged Americans to lend money to the government, financing a large part of the war.

questions.q: The introduction of income tax withholding from paychecks in 1943...
options: Ended the income tax for the duration of the war emergency
Lowered taxes for the working poor only
Banned strikes in the war plants
Made it easier to collect taxes from many more workers
questions.explain: The war pushed millions of Americans onto income tax rolls, and the pay-as-you-go system stayed after the war.

questions.q: "Rosie the Riveter" became a symbol of...
options: Boys collecting scrap in the Scouts
Farm families growing victory gardens
Union leaders in defense plants
Women working in war industries
questions.explain: Millions of women took jobs in factories and shipyards as men entered the military, challenging stereotypes about women's work.

questions.q: The "We Can Do It!" poster, now associated with Rosie the Riveter, was originally created in 1943 for...
options: The Army's drive to draft workers into the war plants
A women's suffrage society
A Red Cross blood drive
A Westinghouse factory to boost morale
questions.explain: The poster was not widely seen at the time, and it became an icon decades later.

questions.q: After the war, many women who had taken wartime jobs...
options: Gained pay equal to men's in all of the factories
Were drafted into the military services
Were pushed to leave jobs for returning veterans, though many stayed
Lost the right to vote in many states
questions.explain: Many wanted to keep working, and women's wartime employment laid groundwork for later changes.

questions.q: The WAC and WAVES, created during World War II, were...
options: Unions for women factory workers and shipyard welders
Aircraft makers owned by women
Women's branches of the Army and the Navy
Spy agencies run by women
questions.explain: Tens of thousands of women served in non-combat roles, freeing men for the front.

questions.q: The WASP (Women Airforce Service Pilots) during World War II...
options: Flew bombing missions over Germany as crew members
Led fighter squadrons in Europe against the German Luftwaffe
