Ferried aircraft and tested planes to free male pilots
Trained as spies for the OSS in London
questions.explain: Over a thousand women flew military planes in the US, but they were not given full military status until the 1970s.

questions.q: The Tuskegee Airmen were...
options: Black pilots trained at Tuskegee, Alabama, who flew for the Army Air Forces
Navy divers who worked on ship salvage in the Pacific theater
Code breakers who worked in Washington, D.C.
Marine snipers who fought on Iwo Jima
questions.explain: They flew escort missions over Europe, and their record challenged racist assumptions about Black military capability.

questions.q: Which fighter, with a famous red-painted tail, is most closely associated with the Tuskegee Airmen's 332nd Fighter Group escorting bombers over Europe?
options: F4U Corsair
P-38 Lightning
P-51 Mustang
Spitfire
questions.explain: The 332nd flew several aircraft but became best known for red-tailed P-51 Mustangs. Praised for protecting bombers, the group's record helped spur the later desegregation of the military.

questions.q: Executive Order 8802, signed by FDR in 1941, did what?
options: Desegregated the entire army and navy at once in 1941
Ended Jim Crow laws throughout the South
Opened the vote to Black Southerners
Banned discrimination in defense industries and created the FEPC
questions.explain: A. Philip Randolph's threat of a march on Washington pushed Roosevelt to act, though enforcement was limited.

questions.q: The "Double V" campaign of the Pittsburgh Courier urged victory against...
options: The Axis and rationing at home
Fascism abroad and racism at home
Hunger and disease around the world
Germany and Japan, with no mention of home
questions.explain: The slogan captured the contradiction of Black soldiers fighting for freedom in a segregated military and nation.

questions.q: The 1943 Detroit race riot was linked to...
options: A fight at a baseball game that spread
Tensions over jobs and housing in crowded wartime cities
A strike by autoworkers at a large Detroit plant that spring
A court ruling about integrating schools
questions.explain: Black and white workers competed in a city swollen by war industry. Federal troops were needed to restore order.

questions.q: The Bracero Program, begun in 1942, brought...
options: Mexican workers on US farms and railroads under temporary contracts
Chinese workers to California orchards for the harvest season
German prisoners of war to Texas farms
Women to shipyards in Oregon and Washington
questions.explain: It addressed labor shortages and continued after the war, though many braceros faced poor pay and treatment.

questions.q: The 1943 Zoot Suit Riots in Los Angeles involved...
options: A strike of dock workers
Servicemen attacking Mexican American youths
A fight over rationing
A protest of Japanese internment by Mexican American leaders
questions.explain: Racial prejudice drove the violence, and police often arrested the victims rather than the attackers.

questions.q: Executive Order 9066, signed by President Roosevelt in February 1942, led to...
options: The wartime draft of young men
The forced removal of Japanese Americans from the West Coast
The rationing of food, gasoline and rubber across the country
A ban on strikes in war plants
questions.explain: The order let the military exclude people from designated areas. About 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most of them US citizens or long-term residents, were forced from their homes and confined in camps.

questions.q: About two-thirds of the people removed from the West Coast under Executive Order 9066 were...
options: US citizens
Immigrants who had arrived after 1930
Merchant seamen from Japan
Japanese government employees
questions.explain: Many were children of immigrants who were born in the United States, and they lost homes, farms and businesses.

questions.q: Manzanar in California and Heart Mountain in Wyoming were...
options: Army bases where recruits trained for the infantry in the South
Training centers for aviators
Camps where Japanese Americans were confined
War factories on the coast
questions.explain: Families lived in barracks behind barbed wire for years, in harsh conditions, often far from their homes.

questions.q: In Korematsu v. United States (1944), the Supreme Court...
options: Struck down the exclusion order as unconstitutional and void
Ordered the camps closed within a year
Required payments to those who had been confined
Upheld the exclusion of Japanese Americans from the Coast
questions.explain: The majority said that military necessity justified the policy. The decision is now widely criticized, and dissenting justices warned of racism.

questions.q: Justice Robert Jackson's dissent in Korematsu warned that...
options: Japan should be punished for the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941
The decision could become a precedent that endangers civil liberties
The army had too little power on the West Coast
Americans of German descent should also be removed
questions.explain: He wrote that the ruling would lie around "like a loaded weapon," ready for any authority claiming urgent need.

questions.q: Which earlier 1943 decision upheld a curfew on Japanese Americans?
options: Hirabayashi v. United States
Plessy v. Ferguson
Schenck v. United States
Muller v. Oregon
questions.explain: The Court limited its decision to the curfew, which set the stage for Korematsu on the exclusion order itself.

questions.q: What did the Supreme Court rule in Ex parte Endo (1944)?
options: The policy of internment was valid in all cases
The army could draft Japanese Americans into combat units
The government could not keep detaining a loyal citizen
Japan had to pay reparations to the United States
questions.explain: The ruling led to the end of the exclusion policy in 1945, though it did not squarely overturn Korematsu.

questions.q: The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, famous for its record in Italy and France, consisted largely of...
options: Native American soldiers
Puerto Rican soldiers
Japanese American soldiers
Black pilots
questions.explain: Many volunteers came from Hawaii and from the incarceration camps. The unit became one of the most decorated for its size and length of service in US history.

questions.q: The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 provided...
options: A ban on any future internment of citizens
The return of the camp land to its former owners in the West
Citizenship for new immigrants from Asia
An apology and payments to surviving Japanese American internees
questions.explain: President Reagan signed the law that followed a congressional commission's finding that the incarceration resulted from prejudice and hysteria.

questions.q: The Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians found in 1983 that internment was caused by...
options: Racial prejudice, war hysteria and failed political leadership
Documented cases of spying by Japanese Americans on the coast
Real military necessity as shown by the evidence
A decision of the federal courts
questions.explain: Its findings, based on records at the National Archives and testimony, laid the foundation for redress.

questions.q: Japanese Americans in Hawaii were not interned in large numbers largely because...
options: They made up a large share of the island workforce
Hawaii had no soldiers of its own to guard the islands
They were all American citizens by birth
The governor refused to cooperate with the army
questions.explain: Mass removal would have crippled the islands' economy, though leaders were targeted for detention.

questions.q: The Truman Committee, led by a senator from Missouri, investigated...
options: The Pearl Harbor attack
Organized crime on the waterfront
Communist influence in Hollywood
Waste and fraud in wartime defense contracts
questions.explain: Harry Truman's committee saved taxpayers a great deal of money and made him a national figure, leading to his vice presidential nomination in 1944.

questions.q: The GI Bill of 1944 provided veterans with...
options: Education benefits, loans for homes and businesses, and unemployment aid
Free farms in the Western states
Lifetime pensions at full pay
Land grants in the West for farmers, as in the Homestead Act
questions.explain: The law helped millions attend college and buy homes, reshaping the postwar middle class, though benefits were unevenly available to Black veterans.

questions.q: The Manhattan Project was...
options: A plan to build new public housing in New York City
A navy program to build carriers
An airlift program for Europe
The secret US program to build the first atomic bombs
questions.explain: Directed by General Leslie Groves with physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer leading the weapons lab, it employed hundreds of thousands in secret sites.

questions.q: The 1939 letter signed by Albert Einstein urging President Roosevelt to consider atomic research warned that...
options: Japan had already built a working atomic bomb
The Soviets were far ahead in atomic research
Uranium supplies were running out worldwide
Nazi Germany might build atomic weapons
questions.explain: The letter, drafted with physicist Leo Szilard, helped lead to the US effort to develop the bomb first.

questions.q: Which New Mexico site hosted the Manhattan Project's weapons laboratory?
options: Roswell
Santa Fe airfield
Taos
Los Alamos
questions.explain: Scientists gathered there in 1943, and the first bomb test, called Trinity, occurred in the New Mexico desert in July 1945.

questions.q: Oak Ridge, Tennessee, and Hanford, Washington, were Manhattan Project sites that...
options: Produced fissile materials such as enriched uranium and plutonium
Trained pilots for the bomber force at Army air bases
Built landing ships for the Navy
Developed radar for aircraft
questions.explain: These secret cities grew quickly and employed workers, many of whom did not know the purpose of their work.

questions.q: The B-29 Superfortress bomber, which dropped the atomic bombs on Japan, was notable for...
options: Long range and a pressurized cabin
Carrying only passengers and mail
Fighting underwater against submarines
Being the first jet-powered bomber
questions.explain: The aircraft could fly high and far, so it could bomb Japan from distant island bases.

questions.q: The B-29 Enola Gay, which dropped the first atomic bomb, is now displayed at...
options: The White House in Washington
Arlington National Cemetery and its Memorial Amphitheater in Virginia
The Pentagon in Arlington
The Smithsonian's Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center in Virginia
questions.explain: The restored aircraft is part of the National Air and Space Museum's collection and illustrates the end of the war.

questions.q: The first atomic bomb used in war was dropped on which Japanese city on August 6, 1945?
options: Hiroshima
Nagasaki
Tokyo
Kyoto
questions.explain: The attack destroyed much of the city and killed tens of thousands immediately, with many more deaths from injuries and radiation.

questions.q: A second atomic bomb was dropped on Nagasaki on...
options: August 6, 1945
September 2, 1945
August 9, 1945
questions.explain: Days later Japan announced its willingness to surrender. The decision to use these bombs remains debated by historians.

questions.q: President Truman explained the decision to use the atomic bomb as an effort to...
options: Test the weapon on a neutral country
Please the Soviet Union before the Potsdam meeting began
End the war quickly and avoid a costly invasion of Japan
Punish China for its alliance with Japan
questions.explain: Truman and his advisers feared very heavy casualties in an invasion, though historians continue to debate whether other options existed.

questions.q: The formal Japanese surrender was signed on September 2, 1945, aboard which ship?
options: USS Arizona
USS Enterprise
USS Maine
USS Missouri
questions.explain: The ceremony in Tokyo Bay ended World War II, which is commemorated as V-J Day in the US.

questions.q: How many granite pillars encircle the plaza of the National World War II Memorial, which opened in 2004?
questions.explain: The 56 pillars represent the 48 states, the District of Columbia and the territories of the time. The two arches stand for the Atlantic and Pacific theaters.

questions.q: The WWII Memorial has two arches that represent...
options: The Atlantic and Pacific theaters of the war
The East and West coasts of the US
The Axis and the Allies
The beginning and the end of the Second World War
questions.explain: Visitors enter between the arches and a central fountain, with a wall of gold stars for those who died.

questions.q: The Freedom Wall of gold stars at the WWII Memorial honors...
options: Americans who died in the war, one star for every 100
Medal of Honor recipients, with one star for each of them
Presidents who led the nation in wartime
Navy ships lost in the Pacific
questions.explain: More than four thousand stars symbolize over 400,000 Americans killed.

questions.q: Approximately how many Americans died in World War II?
options: Over one million
About 58,000
More than 400,000
About 116,000
questions.explain: Roughly 16 million Americans served in the armed forces, and far more civilians in other nations died.

questions.q: Winston Churchill spent weeks at the White House in December 1941, which showed...
options: American neutrality in the European war
A dispute over naval bases in the Caribbean Sea
A drift back toward isolation
The close wartime cooperation of the US and Britain
questions.explain: He and Roosevelt developed the Arcadia strategy, and Churchill addressed Congress during his visit.

questions.q: Which advisor, who lived for a time in the White House, was FDR's closest aide during the war?
options: Harry Hopkins
Harold Ickes
Henry Morgenthau
Cordell Hull
questions.explain: Hopkins managed Lend-Lease and traveled to meet Allied leaders, acting as FDR's personal representative.

questions.q: The Smith-Connally Act of 1943 was passed after...
options: The Pearl Harbor attack, at the request of Roosevelt
Wartime strikes by coal miners, over FDR's veto
A decision of the Supreme Court
A request from the AFL and CIO
questions.explain: The law gave the president authority to take over plants threatened by strikes, and Congress enacted it despite FDR's veto.

questions.q: The National Security Act, which created the National Military Establishment later renamed the Department of Defense, was passed in which year?
questions.explain: Congress merged the War and Navy departments into a national military establishment, led by a Secretary of Defense. It was renamed the Department of Defense in 1949.

questions.q: Which Treasury Department program sold small-denomination savings bonds and stamps to ordinary citizens in World War II?
options: Liberty Loans
Treasury notes for banks
Greenbacks
War bonds
questions.explain: Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau Jr. led campaigns that reached millions of buyers.

questions.q: Which cabinet official led the Treasury through most of the Great Depression and World War II?
options: Andrew Mellon
Henry Morgenthau Jr.
William McAdoo
Henry Wallace
questions.explain: Morgenthau served from 1934 to 1945, and he took part in the Bretton Woods conference.

questions.q: Andrew Mellon, Treasury Secretary under Harding, Coolidge and Hoover, favored...
options: Higher taxes on large fortunes to fund new programs
Large public works spending to fight unemployment
Federal ownership of key industries
Lower taxes, especially on high incomes, and a smaller debt
questions.explain: Mellon believed that tax cuts would spur investment, a policy aligned with the pro-business outlook of the 1920s.

questions.q: The original Treaty of Versailles, signed in 1919 but not ratified by the Senate, is...
options: Not part of US law because the US never approved it
A ratified document held in the National Archives in Washington
The basis of the United Nations Charter
Replaced by the NATO treaty
questions.explain: The US later signed a separate peace with Germany in 1921, since the Senate had voted down the treaty.

questions.q: The Nineteenth Amendment was formally certified on August 26, 1920, by...
options: The president alone
The Speaker
The Secretary of State
The Chief Justice
questions.explain: After Tennessee ratified, Bainbridge Colby signed the proclamation. The original documents are now kept at the National Archives.

questions.q: The National Archives, which hold the originals of key government records, was created by Congress in...
questions.explain: The Archives' building on Constitution Avenue, completed in the 1930s, houses documents ranging from executive orders to treaties.

questions.q: The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery began with the burial of an unidentified soldier from...
options: The Civil War
The Spanish-American War
World War II
World War I
questions.explain: The soldier was interred on November 11, 1921, and the tomb later received unknowns from other wars.

questions.q: Before burial at Arlington, the World War I Unknown Soldier lay in state in...
options: The Lincoln Memorial
The White House
The Capitol Rotunda
The Library of Congress
questions.explain: Thousands of people filed past the casket in November 1921, and President Harding presided at the funeral ceremony.

questions.q: Which president, buried at Arlington, served in the Navy in World War II and was assassinated in 1963?
options: John F. Kennedy
Franklin Roosevelt
Dwight Eisenhower
Harry Truman
questions.explain: Kennedy, who commanded a PT boat in the Pacific, was buried at Arlington National Cemetery with an eternal flame.

questions.q: The Memorial Amphitheater at Arlington, completed in 1920, was built to...
options: Hold meetings of Congress during national emergencies
Serve as a federal courthouse
Host ceremonies such as Memorial Day and later Unknown Soldier services
Store military records
questions.explain: It became the site for the national Memorial Day and Veterans Day observances.

questions.q: Which architect, director of works for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, designed Washington's Union Station, which opened in 1907?
options: Cass Gilbert
Louis Sullivan
Henry Hobson Richardson
Daniel Burnham
questions.explain: Burnham designed the station as part of the City Beautiful movement, which aimed to give American cities grand public buildings and open spaces.

questions.q: Which librarian of Congress, appointed in 1899, expanded the library's role as a national research institution?
options: Ainsworth Spofford
Herbert Putnam
Archibald MacLeish
Daniel Boorstin
questions.explain: Putnam served until 1939 and introduced interlibrary loans and cataloging reforms. Poet Archibald MacLeish followed him.

questions.q: Which Washington, D.C., landmark church building, begun in 1907, is a Gilded Age and Progressive Era symbol of national religious life?
options: St. John's Church
Washington National Cathedral
The Basilica of the Immaculate Conception
Metropolitan AME
questions.explain: Construction of the Gothic-style cathedral began in 1907 and took most of the century, reflecting a vision of a national spiritual center.

questions.q: Which president is buried in Washington National Cathedral?
options: Theodore Roosevelt
Woodrow Wilson
Warren Harding
Calvin Coolidge
questions.explain: Wilson, who died in 1924, is the only president buried in Washington, D.C.; his tomb is in a bay of the cathedral nave.

questions.q: Which twentieth-century Civil Rights leader preached his last Sunday sermon at the National Cathedral in 1968?
options: Whitney Young
Ralph Abernathy
Martin Luther King Jr.
Roy Wilkins
questions.explain: His final sermon at the cathedral, days before his death, tied the building to later civil rights history. Earlier leaders laid foundations.

questions.q: Henry Ford's Highland Park plant is credited with...
options: Making the first airplane
Building tanks and trucks for the army in 1914
Producing the first radios
Introducing the moving assembly line in 1913
questions.explain: The line cut the time to build a car, and Ford's methods were widely imitated.

questions.q: The Kodak Brownie camera of 1900 was important because...
options: It was used mostly by spies and soldiers
It was the first camera to use color film in 1900
It made photography cheap and accessible to ordinary people
It was invented by Thomas Edison
questions.explain: Mass-produced cameras allowed families to take their own photographs, reflecting the growth of consumer culture.

questions.q: Jesse Owens won four gold medals at which 1936 event, challenging Nazi racial claims?
options: The Summer Olympics in Berlin
The Winter Olympics in Garmisch-Partenkirchen
The Pan American Games
The AAU national championships
questions.explain: His victories in Hitler's Germany drew worldwide attention, though he returned to a segregated America.

questions.q: Joe Louis's first-round knockout of Max Schmeling in 1938 was widely celebrated in the United States as...
options: A symbolic victory over Nazi Germany
The end of segregation in professional boxing
A victory of professional boxers over amateurs
The first heavyweight title won by a Black boxer
questions.explain: Louis became a hero to Americans of both races, and the fight was seen as a symbolic contest between democracy and fascism. Jack Johnson had been the first Black heavyweight champion in 1908.

questions.q: Orson Welles's 1938 radio broadcast of The War of the Worlds became famous because...
options: It was a speech by President Roosevelt
It was an official declaration of war
Some listeners thought the alien invasion was real
It was a documentary about the planet Mars and its canals
questions.explain: The program showed radio's power to shape public reaction, though the panic was probably exaggerated.

questions.q: The Hindenburg disaster of 1937 in New Jersey helped end...
options: Atlantic shipping across the ocean
Jet travel in the postwar years
The era of passenger travel by airship
Transcontinental railroads in the American West
questions.explain: The explosion of the German airship, filmed and broadcast, ended public confidence in hydrogen-filled zeppelins.

questions.q: The Japanese Mitsubishi Zero fighter, which shocked American pilots early in the war, was notable for...
options: Its heavy armor plating
Its agility and long range
Its jet engine
Its large size and weight
questions.explain: Early in the war the Zero outmaneuvered many US planes, but American fighters and tactics improved.

questions.q: The B-17 Flying Fortress was used by the US Army Air Forces for...
options: Landing on aircraft carriers in the Pacific
Reconnaissance flights only
Daylight strategic bombing of Germany
Transporting paratroopers
questions.explain: Crews flew dangerous missions over Europe, and many were lost to fighters and flak.

questions.q: The Allied air campaign over Europe included which long-range American escort fighter?
options: Spitfire
Hurricane
Messerschmitt
P-51 Mustang
questions.explain: With extra fuel tanks, it could accompany bombers all the way to Germany, sharply reducing losses.

questions.q: The Civil Air Patrol, founded in 1941, used civilian pilots to...
options: Fight in the skies over Europe against German fighters and bombers
Patrol coasts for submarines and perform support missions
Ferry bombers across the Atlantic to Britain
Train spies for the OSS
questions.explain: Civilian volunteers flew thousands of hours searching for German U-boats off the coast.

questions.q: In which year did the Battle of the Atlantic turn decisively toward the Allies as U-boat losses mounted?
questions.explain: In 1943, convoys, radar, escort carriers and long-range aircraft sank U-boats faster than Germany could build them, while Liberty ships replaced Allied losses.

questions.q: The Liberty ships of World War II were notable because they...
options: Were warships armed with heavy guns
Were mass produced quickly by yards to carry supplies
Were passenger liners used for luxury travel across the Atlantic
Were ships captured from Germany
questions.explain: Henry Kaiser's yards built ships in a matter of weeks using prefabrication, and many women and Black workers joined the labor force.

questions.q: Henry Kaiser, Willow Run and the shipyards of the West Coast illustrate...
options: The huge scale and speed of American wartime production
The failure of American industry to adapt to war needs
Slow mobilization for the war
The end of the peacetime draft
questions.explain: Willow Run produced B-24 bombers at an enormous rate, and the nation's output overwhelmed that of the Axis.

questions.q: The "unconditional surrender" policy and the Allied Declaration of the United Nations in January 1942 show that...
options: The US acted alone against the Axis
The war was almost over
The League of Nations was being reborn in Geneva
The Allies coordinated war aims among many nations
questions.explain: The declaration pledged 26 nations not to make a separate peace, and "United Nations" became the name for the Allied coalition.

questions.q: The Navy's F6F Hellcat fighter was important in the Pacific because it...
options: Was the Navy's first jet fighter
Escorted B-17 bombers over Germany
Served as the Army Air Forces' main transport
Helped US carrier pilots win control of the air in the Pacific
questions.explain: The rugged fighter was built in large numbers and achieved a strong kill ratio against Japanese aircraft, giving the fleet air superiority.

questions.q: Ford's Theatre was restored and reopened as a historic site and working theater in...
questions.explain: It was rebuilt to look like it did in 1865, and today it combines performances with museum exhibits on Lincoln's presidency.

questions.q: What was a major political consequence of Lincoln's assassination in April 1865?
options: Radical Republicans lost control of Congress
The Civil War ended with the president's death
Andrew Johnson became president and clashed with Congress over Reconstruction
Reconstruction ended in the South
questions.explain: Johnson's conflict with Congress led to the Reconstruction Acts of 1867 and to his impeachment in 1868, which shaped the politics of the era.

questions.q: The Lincoln Memorial statue's sculptor, Daniel Chester French, is also known for creating...
options: The Statue of Liberty
Mount Rushmore
The Minute Man statue in Concord, Massachusetts
The Statue of Freedom on the Capitol dome
questions.explain: French's work shows a seated Lincoln, and he worked with the architect Henry Bacon.

questions.q: The elevator of the Washington Monument, which opened the monument to the public in 1888, was run by...
options: A mule
A steam engine
A water wheel
Electric motors
questions.explain: The ride took about ten minutes, and visitors later could climb the stairs.

questions.q: Which 1901 plan, named for a senator from Michigan, shaped the modern National Mall and placed the Lincoln Memorial at its west end?
options: The McMillan Plan
The Burnham Plan
The L'Enfant Plan
The Olmsted Plan
questions.explain: The McMillan Commission revived and extended L'Enfant's design, clearing the Mall and setting the stage for monuments such as the Lincoln Memorial.

questions.q: The Jefferson Memorial was built at the Tidal Basin, a space created from...
options: A natural lake
A Civil War fort
Land reclaimed from the Potomac River in the late 1800s
An old canal
questions.explain: Army engineers dredged the Potomac flats in the late 1800s, creating land that became East Potomac Park and the Tidal Basin, later the site of the cherry trees and monuments.

questions.q: The memorial's engraved words about "eternal hostility against every form of tyranny over the mind of man" come from...
options: The Gettysburg Address
Thomas Jefferson's letter to Benjamin Rush
The Fourteen Points
The Federalist Papers
questions.explain: The passage reflects Jefferson's views on freedom of religion and thought.

questions.q: The National Cathedral's early plans in 1893 came from an act of Congress that chartered...
options: The Smithsonian Institution
The Protestant Episcopal Cathedral Foundation
The Library of Congress
The Federal Reserve
questions.explain: The foundation, chartered in 1893, built the cathedral over decades largely with private gifts.

questions.q: Washington National Cathedral's Bethlehem Chapel was the first part of the church completed, in...
questions.explain: Services began there before the main nave was done, and the cathedral continued to grow for decades.

questions.q: Charles Hamilton Houston's NAACP legal campaign of the 1930s first focused on inequality in which area?
options: Whites-only primaries
Segregated railroad cars
Elementary schools in the Deep South
Graduate and professional schools
questions.explain: Houston's strategy began with state graduate and law schools, producing wins such as Pearson v. Murray (Maryland, 1936) and Missouri ex rel. Gaines v. Canada (1938) that set the stage for Brown v. Board in 1954.

questions.q: In United States v. Wong Kim Ark (1898), the Supreme Court held that a person born in the US to Chinese immigrant parents was...
options: A resident alien until reaching adulthood
A subject of China under the Burlingame Treaty
A citizen under the Fourteenth Amendment
A citizen only if the parents had naturalized
questions.explain: The Court read the Fourteenth Amendment's birth-citizenship clause broadly, even though Chinese immigrants themselves could not become citizens.

questions.q: In the 1879 case of Standing Bear, a federal judge in Nebraska ruled that a Ponca man was...
options: An alien who needed permission to travel
A person under the law with the right to seek a writ of habeas corpus
A ward of the army with no legal standing
A citizen entitled to vote in state elections
questions.explain: The decision recognized that Native people were persons within the meaning of the law, though it did not give them citizenship.

questions.q: The Curtis Act of 1898 extended allotment policy to the Five Tribes in Indian Territory and...
options: Granted each tribal member a federal pension
Moved the Five Tribes to reservations in Kansas
Created new tribal courts with federal judges
Ended their tribal governments' authority as Oklahoma statehood approached
questions.explain: The law dissolved tribal courts and governments, paving the way for Indian Territory to join Oklahoma as a single state in 1907.

questions.q: The Apache leader Geronimo's 1886 surrender is often seen as the end of...
options: The Ghost Dance movement on the Plains
The Dawes Act's allotment program
The war with the Nez Perce in Idaho
The major armed Native resistance in the Southwest
questions.explain: After years of pursuit by US troops, Geronimo and his followers gave up in Arizona Territory and were sent to prisons in Florida and later Oklahoma.

questions.q: Which Lakota leader was killed by Indian police in December 1890 shortly before Wounded Knee?
options: Crazy Horse
Red Cloud
Sitting Bull
Spotted Tail
questions.explain: Officials feared that Sitting Bull would join the Ghost Dance. His death during an attempted arrest added to the tension at Pine Ridge.

questions.q: Fred Harvey's chain of restaurants and hotels along Western railroad lines helped...
options: Replace the Pullman sleeping car
Make long-distance train travel more comfortable and bring settlers westward
Create a national bakery trade
Build the first transcontinental telegraph
questions.explain: The Harvey Houses served meals to rail passengers across the Southwest, and the "Harvey Girls" became a part of Western lore.

questions.q: The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 began when workers on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad protested...
options: The introduction of sleeping cars
A wage cut during a depression
A new schedule of time zones
The hiring of immigrants as engineers
questions.explain: The strike spread to many cities, and violence in places such as Pittsburgh prompted President Hayes to send federal troops.

questions.q: Why did railroad companies create a standardized track width (gauge) across much of the country in the 1880s?
options: To satisfy a Supreme Court order
To let trains travel from one line to another without changing cars
To reduce the use of steel
To follow a law passed by the states
questions.explain: Southern lines converted to the standard gauge in 1886, so cars could run between connected systems without unloading. A uniform gauge strengthened a national market.

questions.q: Greenbacks, the paper currency issued during the Civil War, became a political issue in the 1870s because...
options: They were made of silver
They were issued only in the South
Congress had never authorized them
Debtors wanted to keep them in circulation while creditors wanted a return to gold
questions.explain: The Resumption Act of 1875 returned the nation to the gold standard in 1879, a goal that irritated indebted farmers.

questions.q: What event of 1895 involved J. P. Morgan and President Cleveland?
options: Morgan was named Secretary of the Treasury
Cleveland nationalized Morgan's bank
A syndicate sold gold to the Treasury to protect its reserve
The Treasury adopted free silver
questions.explain: The deal stopped a drain on gold reserves, but critics accused Cleveland of rescuing Wall Street and favoring bankers.

questions.q: When it was finished in 1884, the Washington Monument was briefly...
options: The largest dome in America
The first skyscraper in New York
The oldest federal building
The tallest structure in the world
questions.explain: The obelisk stood about 555 feet high, and it remained the tallest until the Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889.

questions.q: The Washington Monument was dedicated in...
options: 1848, the year work began
1865, just after the Civil War
1900, at the new century
1885, under President Chester Arthur's administration
questions.explain: The monument was dedicated on February 21, 1885, but did not open to the public until 1888, when its steam elevator was installed.

questions.q: In 1874 Frederick Douglass became president of which institution that soon failed?
options: The Freedman's Savings Bank
The Tuskegee Institute
The Bureau of Refugees
The Liberty Party
questions.explain: The bank's collapse that year cost many Black depositors their savings, and Douglass tried to help even though he arrived late.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass's 1893 pamphlet about the World's Columbian Exposition, written with Ida B. Wells and others, protested...
options: The use of electric lighting
The exclusion of Black Americans from the fair's exhibits
The high price of admission
The fair's location in Chicago
questions.explain: The pamphlet criticized how little the fair recognized Black achievement, even as it celebrated national progress.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass's autobiography first published in 1845 was titled...
options: Up from Slavery
Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
The Souls of Black Folk
Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl
questions.explain: The book described his enslavement and escape, becoming a landmark of antislavery writing, and he later wrote revised memoirs.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass died in 1895 after attending a meeting of...
options: The Republican convention
A women's rights council in Washington
The Tuskegee trustees
A Senate hearing
questions.explain: He had long supported women's suffrage and attended the National Council of Women just before his death at Cedar Hill.

questions.q: After the Spanish-American War, the Senate debated annexing the Philippines in part because...
options: Supporters wanted a naval base and a trade foothold in Asia
The islands held oil needed by the Navy
Spain had demanded it in the treaty
Filipinos had asked to become a state
questions.explain: Expansionists such as Roosevelt and Mahan stressed strategic and commercial advantages, while opponents warned of ruling people without consent.

questions.q: Which Gilded Age law is named after Senator John Sherman of Ohio, brother of a Civil War general?
options: The Pendleton Act
The Interstate Commerce Act
The Sherman Antitrust Act
The Dawes Act
questions.explain: The senator also gave his name to a silver purchase act, and his brother William Tecumseh Sherman led the March to the Sea.

questions.q: The "Billion Dollar Congress" of 1889-1891 got its nickname because...
options: It cut spending to a billion dollars
It appropriated more than a billion dollars for the first time in peacetime
It borrowed a billion dollars from banks
It sold a billion acres of land
questions.explain: Under Speaker Reed, Republicans funded pensions, the navy and other programs, and the high spending made them unpopular in 1890.

questions.q: The 1890 pension law of President Benjamin Harrison's Republicans increased federal benefits for...
options: Confederate widows
Union Civil War veterans
Spanish-American War veterans
Revolutionary War soldiers
questions.explain: Pensions became one of the largest items in the federal budget, and Republicans built loyalty among veterans through them.

questions.q: After Reconstruction, which constitutional amendment became the basis for later challenges to Jim Crow in the Supreme Court?
options: The Thirteenth Amendment
The Twelfth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment
The Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection clause
questions.explain: Although the Court limited the amendment in cases like Plessy, it later became the basis for rulings against segregation.

questions.q: Which president, who died in office in 1923, lay in state in the Capitol Rotunda?
options: Calvin Coolidge
Warren G. Harding
Woodrow Wilson
William McKinley
questions.explain: Harding died during a trip to the West Coast, and his body was carried by train to Washington for a public funeral.

questions.q: In July 1915, a bomb damaged the Capitol, set by...
options: An anarchist who wanted to end Prohibition
A mill worker angry at the tariff
A Klansman angry at Congress
A German sympathizer who opposed US arms sales to the Allies
questions.explain: Erich Muenter exploded the bomb in the Senate reception room at night and later tried to kill J.P. Morgan Jr., which showed fears of war spreading to America.

questions.q: The Capitol's Statue of Freedom, placed on the dome in 1863, is the work of...
options: Daniel Chester French
Augustus Saint-Gaudens
Thomas Crawford
Gutzon Borglum
questions.explain: The bronze statue topped the dome built during the Civil War, a symbol of the nation's survival that predates the Gilded Age.

questions.q: In 1919 the House and Senate had both approved the Nineteenth Amendment before it went to...
options: A national referendum
The Supreme Court for review
The states for ratification
The president for a signature
questions.explain: Constitutional amendments need two-thirds of both houses, then approval by three-fourths of the states, and presidents do not sign them.

questions.q: Under the Constitution, bills to raise revenue, such as the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, must begin in the...
options: Senate
Supreme Court
House of Representatives
Cabinet
questions.explain: The House has the power to originate tax measures, and Senate changes to Smoot-Hawley became an area of intense lobbying.

questions.q: The Emergency Banking Act of March 1933 passed the House in about forty minutes and was signed...
options: Two months later
The same day
After the Supreme Court approved it
On Inauguration Day
questions.explain: Members voted on a bill they had not seen in print, and the quick action helped calm the banking crisis.

questions.q: Which House committee created in 1938 to investigate "un-American" activities was led by Martin Dies?
options: The Pecora Committee
The Nye Committee
The Truman Committee
The House Un-American Activities Committee
questions.explain: The committee investigated radicals and critics of the New Deal, and its methods were criticized by civil libertarians.

questions.q: The Volstead Act of 1919, which defined which drinks were illegal, was passed by Congress...
options: With Wilson's strong help
Before the Eighteenth Amendment
After repeal in 1933
Over President Wilson's veto
questions.explain: Wilson objected to wartime enforcement provisions, and Congress overrode the veto to enforce Prohibition.

questions.q: In August 1941, the House extended the draft by a margin of only...
options: Ten votes
Fifty votes
One vote
One hundred votes
questions.explain: The 203-202 vote showed how divided Americans were just months before Pearl Harbor.

questions.q: In 1935 Huey Long of Louisiana became known in the Senate for...
options: Writing the Social Security Act
Chairing the Pecora hearings
A marathon filibuster that lasted about fifteen hours
Leading the Court-packing fight
questions.explain: Long's long speeches included recipes and reading from the Constitution, and he used the platform to promote his Share Our Wealth plan.

questions.q: The Senate's role in confirming Supreme Court justices became prominent when it considered Louis Brandeis in 1916, who was...
options: The first Jewish justice
The first Black justice
The first woman
The first Catholic justice
questions.explain: After a bitter fight in which critics attacked his reform views and his religion, Brandeis was confirmed by a vote of 47 to 22.

questions.q: Franklin Roosevelt appointed Hugo Black, a senator from Alabama, to the Supreme Court in...
questions.explain: Black was FDR's first appointee, and he served until 1971, becoming a major voice on civil liberties despite earlier controversy.

questions.q: A treaty becomes part of US law only after the Senate approves it by...
options: A simple majority
A unanimous vote
A two-thirds vote
A three-fourths vote
questions.explain: The high threshold gave a minority a chance to defeat the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 and 1920.

questions.q: In March 1920, the Senate's last vote on the Treaty of Versailles with reservations failed mainly because...
options: The Supreme Court advised against ratification
Wilson's loyalists would not accept the Lodge reservations
A majority of senators wanted no treaty at all
Lodge refused to allow any vote on the treaty
questions.explain: Without enough support for either version, the treaty never reached the two-thirds required.

questions.q: After Pearl Harbor, the Senate voted on a declaration of war against Japan by a vote of...
options: 96 to 2
82 to 0
questions.explain: The vote was held within hours of President Roosevelt's address, and the House approved with one dissent.

questions.q: Which 1939 Senate leader from Idaho, an isolationist, argued the US should avoid foreign entanglement?
options: Henry Cabot Lodge
William Borah
Robert La Follette
Huey Long
questions.explain: Borah chaired the Foreign Relations Committee and opposed the League of Nations, the World Court and many commitments abroad.

questions.q: The Glass-Steagall Act of 1933 was named for Senator Carter Glass and Representative...
options: Henry Steagall
Hiram Johnson
Robert Wagner
William Borah
questions.explain: The act separated commercial from investment banking and created federal deposit insurance.

questions.q: The Wagner Act was named for Senator Robert Wagner of...
options: New York
Texas
Ohio
California
questions.explain: Wagner also helped write Social Security and other New Deal measures, as one of the Senate's leading liberals.

questions.q: What did the Supreme Court indicate in Gitlow v. New York (1925)?
options: Radical speech has no protection
States cannot punish crimes
Freedom of speech applies to state governments through the Fourteenth Amendment
Congress can ban all newspapers
questions.explain: Although Gitlow lost, the Court's statement began the process of applying Bill of Rights guarantees to the states.

questions.q: In Near v. Minnesota (1931), the Court struck down a state law that allowed...
options: Segregation of public schools
Imprisonment for debt
Limits on rent
Prior restraint of a newspaper
questions.explain: The Court said the government generally cannot prevent publication in advance, a milestone for press freedom.

questions.q: In Missouri ex rel. Gaines v. Canada (1938), the Supreme Court ruled that Missouri...
options: Had to admit a Black student to its law school or provide an equal one in the state
Could close its law school
Could ban Black residents
Had to desegregate all schools
questions.explain: The ruling forced states to take the "equal" part of separate but equal seriously and was part of the NAACP's long legal strategy.

questions.q: Which Chief Justice led the Supreme Court during the New Deal from 1930 to 1941?
options: William Howard Taft
Charles Evans Hughes
Harlan Fiske Stone
Earl Warren
questions.explain: Hughes presided over the 1937 shift in which the Court began upholding New Deal laws.

questions.q: In West Virginia v. Barnette (1943), the Court ruled that public school students...
options: Must salute the flag
Could not be forced to salute the flag
Could be expelled for opposing the war
Must pledge allegiance in church
questions.explain: The Court reversed an earlier decision, saying the government cannot force citizens to declare belief, even during wartime.

questions.q: In Ex parte Quirin (1942), the Supreme Court allowed the government to...
options: Intern American citizens
Draft women
Seize steel mills
Try German saboteurs in a military tribunal
questions.explain: Eight men who landed from submarines were tried quickly by a military commission, and six were executed.

questions.q: United States v. Darby (1941) upheld...
options: The Wagner Act
Social Security
The Fair Labor Standards Act and overruled Hammer v. Dagenhart
The National Recovery Administration
questions.explain: The ruling confirmed Congress's wide power to regulate commerce, ending the old limits that had blocked child labor laws.

questions.q: Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes's "marketplace of ideas" idea appeared in his dissent in...
options: Schenck v. United States
Lochner v. New York
Abrams v. United States
Plessy v. Ferguson
questions.explain: Holmes wrote that truth is best tested in free competition of ideas, a view that influenced later free speech doctrine.

questions.q: Pierce v. Society of Sisters (1925) struck down an Oregon law that...
options: Required children to attend public schools
Banned all night work
Segregated schools
Taxed church property
questions.explain: The law was aimed in part at Catholic schools and reflected the nativism of the 1920s, but the Court protected parents' rights.

questions.q: In Myers v. United States (1926), Chief Justice Taft wrote an opinion saying that...
options: Congress can remove cabinet members
Judges can fire presidents
Governors can remove senators
The president has the power to remove executive officials
questions.explain: Taft, who had been president, favored strong executive authority, though a later case limited the principle for independent agencies.

questions.q: In United States v. Thind (1923), the Supreme Court ruled that an Indian immigrant was not...
options: Allowed to own land
Eligible for the draft
Eligible for naturalization as a "free white person"
Allowed to attend school
questions.explain: The case revealed how race shaped citizenship law, because only "free white persons" could naturalize under the law of the time.

questions.q: The Declaration of Independence and the Constitution were moved to the National Archives in...
questions.explain: They had been kept in the Library of Congress, then were moved in a ceremony in December 1952.

questions.q: The National Archives holds FDR's typed draft of his December 8, 1941, speech, in which he replaced the words 'world history' with...
options: "Disaster"
"Infamy"
"Treachery"
"Tragedy"
questions.explain: He crossed out "world history" and wrote "infamy," a word choice now known worldwide.

questions.q: The Japanese Instrument of Surrender, signed in 1945, is among the documents held by...
options: The National Archives
The Library of Congress
The Smithsonian only
The Supreme Court
questions.explain: The Archives preserves major treaties and surrender documents of the war.

questions.q: The 1890 US census schedules were badly damaged, and later largely discarded, after...
options: A flood on the Potomac
A Senate order to burn them in 1899
A 1921 fire at the Commerce Department building
A war with Spain
questions.explain: A 1921 fire in the Commerce Building destroyed part of the schedules and damaged much of the rest; Congress authorized destroying the remainder in 1933.

questions.q: The 1913 income tax law enacted after the Sixteenth Amendment taxed...
options: Every household at 25 percent
Only corporations
Only inherited wealth
Only a small share of Americans at modest rates
questions.explain: Initially only about 2 percent of households owed any tax, with rates from 1 to 7 percent.

questions.q: The Panic of 1907 was ended in part when J. P. Morgan...
options: Organized bankers to supply cash to failing institutions
Closed the stock exchange for a year
Served as Treasury Secretary
Created the Federal Reserve
questions.explain: The crisis showed the need for a central bank, leading to the Federal Reserve Act of 1913.

questions.q: After President McKinley's assassination in 1901, what new duty did the Treasury Department's Secret Service take on?
options: Policing the Panama Canal Zone
Guarding the gold reserve
Protecting the president
Enforcing the Pure Food and Drug Act
questions.explain: The Secret Service began informal protection of the president around 1902, and Congress formally assigned the job in 1906. The agency had earlier fought counterfeiting.

questions.q: The Silver Purchase Act of 1934 required the Treasury to...
options: Buy silver to increase its role in the money supply
End silver coinage
Sell silver abroad
Melt silver coins
questions.explain: The measure was a concession to Western silver states and farmers who wanted inflation.

questions.q: The Revenue Act of 1935, sometimes called the "wealth tax," raised taxes on...
options: Wages of factory workers
High incomes, large estates and corporations
Sales of consumer goods
Farm land
questions.explain: FDR responded to critics like Huey Long by seeking higher rates on the wealthy, though results were modest.

questions.q: The Aldrich-Vreeland Act of 1908, a response to the Panic of 1907, allowed...
options: Banks to issue emergency currency
Rural free delivery
Higher tariffs
The first income tax
questions.explain: It served as a stopgap and established a commission whose work led to the Federal Reserve System.

questions.q: Which Treasury economist was the chief American architect of the Bretton Woods plan for postwar currencies?
options: Cordell Hull
Henry Morgenthau Jr.
John Maynard Keynes
Harry Dexter White
questions.explain: White drafted the US plan, and Keynes led the British side. Treasury Secretary Morgenthau hosted the 1944 Bretton Woods conference.

questions.q: The Adamson Act of 1916 established...
options: A minimum wage for all workers
The railroad gauge standard
An eight-hour day for railroad workers
National time zones
questions.explain: Congress passed the law to head off a nationwide rail strike, and the Supreme Court upheld it.

questions.q: The streamlined diesel passenger trains of the 1930s, such as the Zephyr, were notable for...
options: Faster speeds and modern design that drew riders in the Depression
Replacing all steam engines
Operating only in the East
Carrying only freight
questions.explain: These trains represented industrial design and attempted to win back travelers from cars and planes.

questions.q: During the Depression, thousands of jobless Americans traveled by hopping freight trains and were called...
options: Hobos
Doughboys
Muckrakers
Wobblies
questions.explain: Many young men left home to seek work, riding rails across the country despite the dangers.

questions.q: The Railway Labor Act of 1926 was passed to...
options: Ban all strikes
Create a national railroad
Set up a process to settle railroad labor disputes
Fix the price of rail tickets
questions.explain: It encouraged collective bargaining and mediation, and it covered railroad employees, who were key to the Pullman porters' campaign.

questions.q: The Orphan Train movement, which ended in 1929, moved children...
options: From farms to cities
From Europe to Canada
From the South to the North
From eastern cities to families in the Midwest and West
questions.explain: Charities placed well over 100,000 children by rail between 1854 and 1929, and the program was later criticized for its harsh conditions.

questions.q: In 1908 the Wright brothers demonstrated their airplane to the Army at...
options: West Point, New York
Fort Myer, Virginia
Fort Sill, Oklahoma
Annapolis, Maryland
questions.explain: The army trials ended in a crash that killed Lieutenant Thomas Selfridge, but a later test led the Army to buy its first airplane.

questions.q: The Army bought its first airplane in 1909 from...
options: Glenn Curtiss
Lockheed
The Wright brothers
Boeing
questions.explain: The Wright Military Flyer was the world's first military aircraft, and it is now held by the Smithsonian.

questions.q: Robert Goddard's 1926 flight in Massachusetts was the first launch of...
options: A jet plane
A helicopter
A liquid-fueled rocket
A balloon
questions.explain: Goddard's experiments laid the groundwork for later rocketry, though he was often ignored in his time.

questions.q: In 1919 a US Navy flying boat made the first flight across the Atlantic, with stops, called the...
options: NC-4
Spirit of St. Louis
Enola Gay
Flyer
questions.explain: The NC-4 flew from Newfoundland by way of the Azores to Lisbon and then to Plymouth, England, in May 1919, years before Lindbergh's solo nonstop flight.

questions.q: The Air Mail Service began in 1918 as part of the...
options: Post Office Department
Navy
Treasury
Supreme Court
questions.explain: Pilots carried mail between Washington, Philadelphia and New York, and the service later led to a national airway system.

questions.q: The National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, set up by Congress in 1915, was the predecessor of...
options: The CIA
NASA
The FAA
The Air Force
questions.explain: The agency conducted research that improved American aircraft, and it was replaced by NASA in 1958.

questions.q: Which Air Force general led the Army Air Forces in World War II and was later made a five-star officer?
options: Curtis LeMay
Jimmy Doolittle
George Patton
Henry "Hap" Arnold
questions.explain: Arnold led the Army Air Forces as it grew from a small prewar force into one of more than two million people, and he was later named General of the Air Force.

questions.q: What were Pan American's long-range flying boats of the 1930s called?
options: Zeppelins
Clippers
Spitfires
Dreadnoughts
questions.explain: The Clippers carried passengers over the Pacific and Atlantic, shrinking the world and becoming a symbol of global reach.

questions.q: Which US airfield in Alabama trained the Tuskegee Airmen?
options: Fort Myer
Moton Field
Wright Field
Kitty Hawk
questions.explain: Moton Field, near Tuskegee Institute, was the site of primary flight training for the Black pilots.

questions.q: William Howard Taft, buried at Arlington National Cemetery in 1930, was the first...
options: General of the Army
President laid to rest there
Woman laid to rest there
Unknown Soldier
questions.explain: John F. Kennedy was the second president buried at Arlington.

questions.q: General John J. Pershing, who led US forces in World War I, was buried at...
options: Arlington National Cemetery
West Point
Mount Vernon
The Capitol
questions.explain: He died in 1948 and lies among the rows of soldiers, as he had requested.

questions.q: Arlington Memorial Bridge, which opened in 1932, links the Lincoln Memorial to...
options: The White House
The Capitol
Mount Vernon
Arlington National Cemetery
questions.explain: The bridge was meant to symbolize the reunion of North and South after the Civil War.

questions.q: Which hero of the Spanish-American War is entombed in the Washington National Cathedral?
options: Chester Nimitz
William Halsey
Richard Byrd
George Dewey
questions.explain: The admiral who destroyed the Spanish fleet at Manila Bay was first buried at Arlington National Cemetery and was later reinterred in the cathedral.

questions.q: General George C. Marshall, who is buried at Arlington, later...
options: Became president of the United States
Served as vice president
Served as Secretary of the Navy
Won the Nobel Peace Prize for the Marshall Plan
questions.explain: He served as Secretary of State and Secretary of Defense, and was honored for helping rebuild Europe.

questions.q: During World War II about how many Americans served in the armed forces?
options: About 1 million
About 16 million
About 3 million
About 50 million
questions.explain: The huge mobilization required enormous organization, which the Pentagon helped manage.

questions.q: The Women's Army Corps, created in 1942 and later with full status, assigned women to...
options: Non-combat jobs like clerks, drivers and technicians
Front-line infantry
Naval vessels
Bomber crews
questions.explain: About 150,000 women served in the WAC, freeing men for combat roles.

questions.q: When it was completed in 1943, the Pentagon was the...
options: First federal building in Virginia built of marble
First skyscraper in Arlington County
World's largest office building by floor area
Tallest building in Washington
questions.explain: The five-story headquarters in Arlington, Virginia, held tens of thousands of workers (about 33,000 at its wartime peak) and remains one of the largest office buildings in the world.

questions.q: The Selective Service System drafted about how many men in World War II?
options: About 100,000
About 10 million
About 500,000
About 50 million
questions.explain: Most of the army's soldiers and many sailors came through the draft.

questions.q: About how many Native Americans served in the US military during World War II?
options: About 44,000
About 4,000
About 400,000
About 1,000
questions.explain: Many served in the Pacific, and others worked in defense jobs at home.

questions.q: Jim Thorpe, a Sac and Fox athlete, won two gold medals at the 1912 Olympics but...
options: Was never recognized
Was hired by Carlisle as coach
Retired at once
Was stripped of them in 1913 over amateur rules
questions.explain: The medals were restored by the Olympic Committee in 1983, decades after his death.

questions.q: The Society of American Indians, founded in 1911, was notable for...
options: Opposing citizenship
Supporting the Dawes Act
Following Boy Scout rules
Being among the first national Native-led reform groups
questions.explain: Its members, many educated at boarding schools, pushed for citizenship and rights.

questions.q: The Osage murders of the 1920s occurred because...
options: The Osage opposed the draft
Settlers wanted farmland
Osage people held oil rights that made some families wealthy
The Osage left the reservation
questions.explain: The killings of Osage people for their headrights led to a major early FBI investigation.

questions.q: Native American veterans of World War I were granted citizenship by...
options: The Dawes Act
A treaty with Britain
A Supreme Court order
An act of Congress in 1919
questions.explain: The law covered veterans who had served, and the Citizenship Act of 1924 extended citizenship to everyone born in the US.

questions.q: Ira Hayes, a Pima Marine who was among the flag-raisers at Iwo Jima, was a member of the...
options: Navajo Nation
Cherokee Nation
Gila River Indian Community
Lakota Nation
questions.explain: After the war, he struggled with fame and with the way his community was treated.

questions.q: The Navajo Code Talkers' code was kept classified until...
questions.explain: After declassification, the Talkers received public honors and later a Congressional Gold Medal.

questions.q: At the 1922 dedication of the Lincoln Memorial, Chief Justice William Howard Taft...
options: Declared war
Gave the main address
Unveiled the statue
Presented it to President Harding as chair of the Lincoln Memorial Commission
questions.explain: As chairman of the Lincoln Memorial Commission, Taft presented the memorial to President Harding, who accepted it for the nation. Robert Todd Lincoln, Lincoln’s only surviving son, attended.

questions.q: The Lincoln Memorial dedication was held on...
options: July 4, 1876
February 12, 1909
August 28, 1963
questions.explain: The memorial opened on Memorial Day, 1922, 57 years after Lincoln's death.

questions.q: The cherry trees around the Tidal Basin near the Jefferson Memorial were a gift from...
options: Paris, in 1886
Seoul, in 1948
Rome, in 1900
The city of Tokyo, in 1912
questions.explain: Mayor Yukio Ozaki's gift helped make cherry blossoms a Washington tradition.

questions.q: The bronze statue of Jefferson at his memorial was installed in 1947, after World War II, because...
options: It was lost at sea
The statue was first made of plaster while metal was needed for the war
Congress withheld funds
It was stolen
questions.explain: The memorial was dedicated in 1943, with a temporary plaster figure.

questions.q: President Theodore Roosevelt took part in a 1907 ceremony to...
options: Dedicate the Panama Canal
Sign the Antiquities Act
Break ground at the Pentagon
Lay the foundation stone of Washington National Cathedral
questions.explain: The cathedral was not finished until 1990, after more than eight decades of construction.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass's 1852 Independence Day address in Rochester is commonly known by which title?
options: The Price of Liberty
What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?
Ain't I a Woman?
Am I Not a Man and a Brother?
questions.explain: In the speech Douglass asked, 'What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?' It is read in classrooms today for its bitter honesty about slavery.
